📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Hospital ratings have become an key resource for choosing where to receive care. They influence which doctors patients choose, how far they are willing to travel, and whether they seek care at a different facility.

On October 27, Healthgrades announced the recipients of the 2027 Specialty Excellence Outpatient Awards and Specialty State Rankings.

In a recent development, the annual awards recognize hospitals delivering outstanding patient outcomes in specialty care across the United States. Healthgrades is the leading platform used by Americans for finding a doctor or hospital.

New research from Healthgrades highlights that hospital quality is increasingly a factor in healthcare decisions.

Around 80% of patients report that when looking for a doctor, the quality of the hospital where they practice matters. Additionally, 7 in 10 patients (68%) say they’re more likely to seek care for a procedure or health condition from a doctor who works at a hospital with high quality ratings.

What’s more, around 71% of patients say they would switch doctors to gain access to a higher-rated hospital.

“Our specialty awards identify the nation’s top-performing hospitals across numerous medical specialties, helping consumers find high quality care tailored to their specific needs,” said Alana Biggers, MD, MPH, medical advisor at Healthgrades.

Healthgrades is owned by RVO Health. By clicking on this link, we may receive a commission. Learn more.

Sources indicate that “Navigating the complex healthcare system can feel daunting, but taking a proactive stance to understand where to access superior care can enhance your healthcare journey and overall experience. The ability to make informed decisions about your health — and where to get care — is a cornerstone of self-advocacy, and we are proud to help make that information accessible to all patients.”.

Healthgrades identifies hospitals that deliver exceptional outcomes across common outpatient procedures and specialty conditions.

Finding high quality care is important, particularly amid a growing gap between top-performing and one-star hospitals.

According to Healthgrades, from 2023 to 2025, if all hospitals had performed at the five-star level from 2023 to 2025:.

“One of the biggest challenges is balancing increasing patient needs with the resources available to healthcare professionals,” Biggers said.

“Hospitals face workforce shortages, growing administrative responsibilities, financial pressures, and increasing complexity in patient care. Physicians and other healthcare professionals need adequate time and support not only to evaluate and treat patients, but also to communicate results, coordinate follow-up care, and address concerns that arise between visits,” she continued.

“When healthcare teams are adequately supported, they are better positioned to communicate effectively with patients, coordinate care, and address patients’ needs.”.

Biggers mentioned that ensuring equal access to quality healthcare is challenging because of factors such as:.

Sources indicate that hospital closures and reduced services make access even more difficult. Biggers identified a few possible solutions, such as expanding outpatient care, building community partnerships, using telehealth when appropriate, and improving coordination among healthcare providers.

According to recent reports, “Ultimately, providing high quality care requires more than clinical expertise. It requires healthcare systems to invest in their workforce, strengthen care coordination, and create environments where healthcare professionals have the resources they need to provide safe, effective, and patient-centered care,” Biggers stated.

“Equally notable, healthcare systems must ensure that patients have meaningful access to these services, regardless of where they live or their socioeconomic circumstances.”.

Healthgrades acknowledges hospitals that excel in three aspects of specialty care:.

Biggers stated that outstanding hospitals recognize that high quality care extends beyond just treating an illness.

“It involves listening to patients, understanding their individual circumstances, and ensuring they feel respected, informed, and involved in their healthcare decisions,” she noted.

Patients want to find a hospital that excels in the procedures or health conditions relevant to them.

The recipients of the Specialty Excellence Awards are among the top 15% of hospitals specializing in these areas.

Healthgrades evaluated patient outcomes at roughly 4,500 hospitals across 31 common procedures and conditions to reach their decisions.

Among the list of Specialty Excellence Award recipients, Healthgrades also recognizes America’s 100 Best Hospitals for Specialty Care for 11 specialty areas andAmerica’s 50 Best Hospitals for Specialty Care for four specialty areas.

“An outstanding hospital prioritizes both patient care and the people delivering that care,” Biggers told Healthline.

“While clinical outcomes, patient safety, and access to evidence-based treatments are essential measures of quality, I believe hospitals must also invest in workforce development and support. This means ensuring physicians, nurses, and other healthcare professionals have appropriate staffing levels, adequate clinical and administrative support, and opportunities for continued professional development,” she continued.

Industry observers note that healthgrades awards U.S. hospitals that excel at Outpatient Orthopedic Surgery, Outpatient Joint Replacement, andOutpatient Prostate Care.

In a recent development, outpatient care is one of the fastest-growing areas of healthcare. The number of orthopedic procedures performed in an outpatient environment has grown exponentially in recent years.

From 2020 to 2025, outpatient hip replacement procedures grew by 81%, while inpatient procedures dropped by 75%. Outpatient knee replacements increased by 71% while inpatient volumes decreased by 70%.

“I believe several factors are contributing to the growing demand for outpatient care, including advances in medical technology, a greater emphasis on preventive care, and the increasing need to manage chronic medical conditions,” Biggers said.

Industry observers note that “Many services and procedures that previously required hospitalization can now be safely performed in outpatient settings. Patients also appreciate the convenience of receiving care closer to home and avoiding unnecessary hospital stays,” she added.

To meet the increasing demand for outpatient procedures, Biggers cautioned that healthcare systems must ensure that these services are adequately staffed and supported.

“Effective communication and coordination between outpatient providers, specialists, and hospitals are essential to maintaining continuity and quality of care,” she mentioned.

State Rankings identify the top three or five hospitals in eligible states across 19 key specialty areas.

Healthgrades is owned by RVO Health. By clicking on this link, we may receive a commission. Learn more.

The rankings are based on clinical performance and build on the 2027 Healthgrades Specialty Excellence Awards Methodology.

State-level specialty care rankings help consumers find outstanding local hospitals for their condition or procedure.

The analysis used Medicare inpatient data from the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) from 2023 to 2025, and assessed patient outcomes across 31 conditions and procedures.

These outcomes served as the foundation for determining Specialty Excellence Awards and state hospital rankings.

With consumer-facing awards and ratings influencing healthcare decisions, transparency about their methods and limitations remains essential.

Ratings can help patients ask better questions and compare options, but they should complement — not replace — clinical guidance and informed decision making.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

BYD unveiled the Yangwang Altior, its latest ultra-luxury EV with coach doors, over 1,000 km of CTLC range, a 1,000V fast-charging platform, and plenty of premium extras.

The “super-luxury executive flagship sedan,” as BYD calls it, made its official debut in Abu Dhabi, UAE, over the weekend.

For those who don’t know, Yangwang is BYD’s ultra-luxury sub-brand, sitting at the very top of its brand hierarchy.

The Atrio is Yangwang’s largest and most luxurious sedan, set to compete with high-end brands like Rolls-Royce, Bentley, and Mercedes-Benz Maybach.

Measuring 5,600 mm long, 2,030 mm wide, and 1,590 mm tall, with a 3,500 mm wheelbase, BYD’s flagship sedan sits squarely between the Rolls-Royce Ghost and Phantom (standard wheelbase) in length.

BYD stated the “Golden Body Proportions” are designed to maximize interior space for both front and rear passengers.

Its meticulous front-end design is inspired by “Ding,” a traditional ancient Chinese cauldron, featuring “diamond-cut” headlights, a 137-gemstone dot-matrix grille, and, to top it off, a 24K pure gold car emblem sits up front and center.

The coach doors create a grand entrance, with the front doors opening at an 80-degree angle and the rear doors opening to a 90-degree angle.

Inside, the flagship sedan takes luxury up a notch with a massive, full-length panoramic center infotainment screen that extends from the driver to the passenger side.

The “Wrap-around cockpit” is designed to create an immersive, premium experience, with four executive seats and a central island for rear passengers that includes vehicle controls, storage, and even a champagne glass holder.

BYD mentioned it offers the most second-row space in its class, but didn’t reveal specifics. The zero-gravity “cloud-like” rear seats feature a four-ball mechanical massage head, you know, for those longer trips.

Meanwhile, the front passenger seat can fold at the push of a button to open up more space for rear passengers.

The interior features premium materials, including full-grain genuine leather seats, diamond-cut detailing, real wood trim, and natural lambswool foot pads.

Industry observers note that and that’s not all. It also has a 39-speaker Dynaudio Platinum Evidence high-end sound system that creates an immersive 360-degree “hall-level” sound experience.

The Yangwang Altio is packed with BYD’s latest breakthrough tech, including a high-speed tire-blowout stability system, emergency float mode, and in-place U-turn or tank-turn control using its quad-motor e4 platform.

It's main rival is the Maextro S800, which wasn't in the list.

It also uses BYD’s second-generation Blade Batteries and Fast Charging Technology, which provides a CLTC driving range of over 1,000 km (621 miles).

Sources indicate that the flagship sedan features “extremely fast flash charging,” BYD remarked, thanks to its 1000V ultra flash charging tech. It takes just five minutes to charge the vehicle’s battery from 10% to 70%. To go from 10% to 97% it takes just nine minutes.

BYD opened orders for the limited-edition “Mountain and River Rhyme” Yangwang Altrio model, which will be extremely exclusive with just 399 units.

Buyers can place a reservation with a 300,000 yuan ($45,000) deposit. BYD didn’t reveal final prices, but the global version is expected to start at around 2 million yuan ($300,000).

Polar bears are gathering close to this Canadian town—and co-existing with humans

📅 08 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (473 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Popsci

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, polar bears (Ursus maritimus) are typically solitary creatures.
  • “It’s an incredible phenomenon to experience,” Alysa McCall, director of science at Polar Bears International (PBI), tells Popular Science.
  • Recent findings suggest that sea ice platforms help polar bears catch seals, which are their main source of prey.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, polar bears (Ursus maritimus) are typically solitary creatures. But in a Canadian town on Hudson Bay, the predators gather along the coast every fall to wait for the ice to freeze.

“It’s an incredible phenomenon to experience,” Alysa McCall, director of science at Polar Bears International (PBI), tells Popular Science. “The bears return to this stretch of coast because it’s where the Bay freezes first, thanks to freshwater from the Churchill River plus the Bay’s currents and winds.”.

Recent findings suggest that sea ice platforms help polar bears catch seals, which are their main source of prey. It’s usually harder for them to do so without the ice, as exemplified in a video PBI captured of a bear on the shore unsuccessfully trying to hunt a seal in the water.

Sources indicate that this makes polar bears particularly vulnerable to climate change, which is bringing about longer ice-free seasons. In fact, polar bears in the Western Hudson Bay subpopulation today are stuck on land for around one month longer than their grandparents. What’s more, their numbers have approximately halved since 1979 because of sea ice loss.

Sources indicate that nicknamed the Polar Bear Capital of the World, the residents of Churchill, Manitoba have front-row seats to the annual polar bear gathering (you can also watch through their Polar Bear Live Cams). They are thus also exposed to conflict with these very large temporary neighbors, and climate change is extending this potentially dangerous overlap.

In a recent development, “When polar bears are on land, they are generally fasting. They sometimes venture into towns and communities to look for food, and human areas are full of things that attract curious bears – from trash bins to food smells,” McCall explains. “As climate change causes polar bears to spend more time on land, they have more opportunities to encounter people.”.

In a recent development, as such, McCall and her colleagues at PBI have developed fresh tools to facilitate human-polar bear coexistence. One of them—cheekily named Bear-dar—is a medium-range polar bear detection radar currently being used at the Eureka Weather Station in Nunavut, Canada. Now the team is testing Bear-vision, a smart polar bear detection camera, at Churchill’s waste facility. According to McCall, it’s cheaper and simpler to use than Bear-dar, and works like a doorbell camera that warns you if there’s a polar bear hanging out outside.

According to recent reports, “The team hopes to make the technology open-source so that Bear-vision will be widely available and accessible. More bear-safe tools mean fewer negative encounters, ultimately keeping people and polar bears separate and safer,” says McCall. “What’s happening along Hudson Bay shows how much communities can do to live harmoniously with nature.”.

#5447. Beyond Us Versus Them

Beyond Us Versus Them

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1068 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Psychologytoday

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Posted November 16, 2026 | Reviewed by Michelle Quirk.
  • In a recent development, on election day this month, Democrats won control of both the House and the Senate, stripping Republicans of a supermajority.
  • Whether or not you’re a fan of Talarico, he might be on to something.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Posted November 16, 2026 | Reviewed by Michelle Quirk.

In a recent development, on election day this month, Democrats won control of both the House and the Senate, stripping Republicans of a supermajority. Headlines surrounding the midterms focused on the rising tension between Democrats and Republicans amid the Trump administration, which has created a lot of rifts between neighbors, friends, and even family members across the country. After winning his race, Democratic U.S. Senator-Elect James Talarico of Texas pleaded with Americans to reframe the narrative, not as a "left versus right" ideological struggle, but as a "top versus bottom" economic divide between wealthy elites and working-class people.

Whether or not you’re a fan of Talarico, he might be on to something. The idea of “us versus them” is as old as the human race, and likely comes from our propensity to form categories. The ability to categorize is a natural and automatic part of the human brain; it allows us to store an incredible amount of information in our memories and make inferences about things we’ve never seen before. Imagine for a second that we didn’t have the ability to form categories; it would mean that every time we encountered a brand-new object, we’d have to learn about it from scratch. The fact that we have categories means that whenever we encounter an apple, for example, we can apply what we know about other apples and safely assume that this new apple is a piece of fruit that tastes sweet and is nutritious. Likewise, whenever we encounter a new dog, we’d know something about the way it likely behaves, what it eats, and whether it’s safe to approach.

Our propensity to categorize starts very early in our lives. By 2 months of age, infants can distinguish broad categories of animate versus inanimate objects. By 3 to 4 months, infants can make basic-level categories for things like cats, dogs, and birds, and by 6 to 7 months they can even form subordinate categories distinguishing among different types of dogs (e.g., Beagles versus St. Bernards). By 14 to 18 months, they can use an object’s function to form categories (even in the absence of physical similarity), and they begin to use labels to organize categories. Needless to say, categorization develops quite early in our lives and over time becomes automatic.

Industry observers note that but despite its benefits, our natural propensity to categorize has some downsides when we extend the ability beyond the categorization of objects to the categorization of people. When we form categories for groups of people, we can easily make false assumptions about someone latest purely based on their category membership. This behavior is the very definition of “prejudice,” which is the tendency to make assumptions about someone purely based on their membership in a particular group. On top of that, when people tend to place themselves in a group, or what we might call an “ingroup,” there will inevitably be others who are left out of that group—people we call “outgroup” members. Infants begin to do this based on perceptual features like gender and race by 6 months, and slightly older children expect that people in the same group—usually marked in research by sharing some arbitrary feature, like a shirt color—should like the same things and behave in similar ways (e.g., Liberman, Woodward, & Kinzler, 2017).

Industry observers note that why is this important? Not surprisingly, we treat people better when we think they’re part of our ingroup, even if that ingroup is completely arbitrary. For example, in a recent set of studies, researchers put adults in groups based on an arbitrary similarity (e.g., people who like green versus blue, or people who prefer squares versus triangles), along with more meaningful ones (e.g., political orientation, religious affiliation, ethnicity), and then had them play a game that required cooperation. The researchers found that the more group memberships people shared—regardless of whether they were meaningful groups or were completely arbitrary—the more people cooperated with each other (Uğurlar et al., 2024). And the fact that we cooperate more with group members who share commonalities with us that are completely trivial suggests that membership isn't necessarily fixed.

And in fact, the boundaries between “us” and “them” can shift depending on which aspects of our identities we emphasize. I've experienced this firsthand. I was only a 21-year-old college student on September 11, 2001, when the planes hit the World Trade Center in Fresh York. Despite it being the scariest day of my life, I remember hundreds of students gathering on the quad, arms around each other’s shoulders, swaying and singing America the Beautiful. I never felt togetherness like that before, and I’m not sure if I’ve ever felt it since. During that tragedy, we weren’t Democrats and Republicans; we were all Americans. We were forced to reframe the ingroup that day—instead of being in separate smaller circles, we made the circle wider.

In real-life research testing this observation, researchers conducted a series of studies where they made participants’ American identity more salient (e.g., by writing a paragraph on why they are proud to identify as American). At the end of the exercise, both Democrat and Republican participants evaluated members of the opposing party more positively (Levendusky, 2018).

Sources indicate that so perhaps one way to move past the “us versus them” mentality in politics, or in life more broadly, is to stop thinking about people as Republicans versus Democrats and instead, to find something you have in common—maybe you are fellow parents, fellow community members, fellow music lovers, or just fellow humans. As Talarico alluded to, by reframing our ideas of group membership—by defining our groups more broadly instead of narrowly—people who might otherwise seem different can now become members of a shared community.

Sources indicate that liberman, Z., Woodward, A. L., & Kinzler, K. D. (2017). The origins of social categorization. Trends in Cognitive Sciences, 21(7), 556–568.

Industry observers note that levendusky, M. S. (2018). Americans, not partisans: Can priming American national identity reduce affective polarization? The Journal of Politics, 80(1), 59–70.

It has been revealed that uğurlar, P., Dorrough, A. R., Isler, O., Yilmaz, O., et al. (2024). Shared group memberships mitigate intergroup bias in cooperation. Social Psychological and Personality Science, 16(2).

💡 Key Takeaways

  • You might find yourself engaging in doomscrolling right before you go to bed, first thing after waking up, standing in line on the subway platform, or even—this is how bad it’s gotten—sitting at the dinner table with the family.
  • It doesn’t have to be this way though.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that doomscrolling: To spend an inordinate amount of time swiping up and down across multiple social media and news feeds—without really getting anything of use out of it. In fact, as addictive as it is, doomscrolling often leaves us feeling worse about ourselves and the world than when we started.

You might find yourself engaging in doomscrolling right before you go to bed, first thing after waking up, standing in line on the subway platform, or even—this is how bad it’s gotten—sitting at the dinner table with the family.

It doesn’t have to be this way though. There are tools and tactics you can use to beat doomscrolling and spend less time on your phone—which means more time enjoying the world and the people around you (and catching up on your sleep). Here are nine tips that can help, across all makes and models of phone.

Recent findings suggest that A grayscale interface can make your phone less distracting. On Android, open Settings and pick Digital Wellbeing > Bedtime Mode to automatically switch to grayscale at a certain time, or enable it manually via Accessibility > Color and motion > Color correction.

Recent findings suggest that on an iPhone, open Settings then choose Accessibility > Display & Text Size > Color Filters to find the grayscale option. There’s no automatic evening color drain like there is on Android, but you can automate the switch by using the Shortcuts app built into iOS.

Both Android and iOS now include tools for setting limits on the time you can spend inside particular apps each day. You can of course easily choose to disable these limits whenever you like, but it might still go some way to weaning you off your doomscrolling habits.

Industry observers note that on Android, from Settings head to Digital Wellbeing > App timers to start choosing your apps and your time limits. Over on iOS, from Settings it’s Screen Time > App & Website Activity to do the same. You could even try slowly reducing your limits over time.

Industry observers note that you might not have noticed, but there are now a wealth of apps to help wean you off unhealthy phone habits, and make sure you keep on top of your screen time. They all gamify the process in some way, encouraging and rewarding you for not doomscrolling.

Some of our favorites include Forest (for Android and iOS), Focus Friend (for Android and iOS), and Focus Traveller (for iOS): They use growing trees, helping a bean character, and hiking up a mountain, respectively, to help you stay on task and avoid distractions.

It has been revealed that pause Point is a new feature available now in Android 17 on Pixel devices, and potentially rolling out more widely in the future. You can find it by opening Settings and choosing Digital Wellbeing > Pause Point, then tapping Continue to get the feature configured.

For the apps that you choose, every time you open them up, you get one of your selected pause points. They include breathing exercises, and custom photo galleries, and the idea is to take a beat and consider if you really need to open up that distracting app after all.

Sources indicate that sometimes the apps and options on your phone aren’t enough on their own. If that’s the case, try the Brick: It’s a $59 physical dongle that uses NFC tech, and when you tap your phone against it, it enables a custom quiet mode that blocks certain websites and apps.

Recent findings suggest that the idea is that the Brick essentially bricks your phone for certain periods, so you spend less time on it. It’s not the only gadget that does this trick either—you could also check out the Autonomous Key, which can be yours for a mere $19 and works along similar lines.

Industry observers note that both Android and iOS let you use so-called Focus modes to cut down on distractions and reduce the temptation to doomscroll. They work like a Do Not Disturb mode with extras, and you can configure different settings for sleeping, driving, or trying to get work done.

On Android, open Settings and then head to Modes; on iOS, it’s Settings and then Focus. The features work in a similar way on both platforms, letting you edit an existing Focus mode or start your own from scratch, with exemptions for certain apps and contacts.

Certain apps come with their own features for limiting the amount of time you spend in them, so it’s worth having a look through the apps that cause you to doomscroll the most to see what options you’ve got—even if it’s just dialing down the number of notifications.

Instagram is one example. Open up the profile tab, then tap the menu button (three horizontal lines) and pick Time management. From the next screen you can set yourself a daily limit, and enable a sleep mode (when notifications are muted) for specific times.

Sources indicate that this is just for the Samsung Galaxy owners out there, and if your phone has the latest One UI 9 software installed on it, there’s a latest tool available in it called AI Network Guard. It’s designed for kids, but it works well for keeping adults (i.e. you) off distracting apps too.

It’s well hidden though: From Settings, tap Connections > Wi-Fi, then the three dots in the corner. Then, tap Intelligent Wi-Fi five times to bring up the Connectivity labs entry. Here you’ll find AI Network Guard, and can choose the apps to impose usage restrictions on.

This is a classic, because the fewer notifications you get, the less likely you are to pick up your phone. There are now a host of ways to tweak alerts on both Android and iOS, but essentially it’s about limiting how and when your apps can interrupt what you’re doing.

According to recent reports, on Android or iOS, choose Notifications from Settings to see the options open to you. You can make alerts less distracting or disable them altogether, on an app-by-app basis, and access useful features like notification snoozing (Android) or scheduled summaries (iOS).

6 to 8 Cups of Tea Daily May Reduce Heart Disease Risk by 11%

📅 28 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (618 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Healthline

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that people who regularly drink tea may have an 11% lower overall risk of vascular disease, which includes conditions such as stroke, heart disease, and peripheral artery disease.
  • Both black tea and green tea may offer heart health benefits.
  • The lowest overall vascular risk was seen among tea drinkers who were also physically active and didn’t smoke.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that people who regularly drink tea may have an 11% lower overall risk of vascular disease, which includes conditions such as stroke, heart disease, and peripheral artery disease. This is according to a study published on October 21 in the Journal of Internal Medicine.

Both black tea and green tea may offer heart health benefits. However, the study reveals an association rather than proving that drinking tea prevents cardiovascular disease.

The lowest overall vascular risk was seen among tea drinkers who were also physically active and didn’t smoke.

The study followed 485,934 people ages 30–79 from the China Kadoorie Biobank for an average of 9 years.

According to recent reports, the researchers found that regular tea drinkers had an 11% lower overall risk of vascular disease compared with those who did not regularly drink tea. They also observed a 37% lower risk of ischemic stroke and a 17% lower risk of heart attack.

There was no clear link for hemorrhagic stroke or pulmonary heart disease.

Among people who drank tea at least weekly, the lowest estimated risk was seen in those consuming approximately 6–8 cups per day. However, the findings do not establish this as a recommended daily intake.

Amit Blumfield, MD, a cardiologist with Manhattan Cardiology in NYC who wasn’t involved in the study, told Healthline that it is crucial to remember this is observational data.

Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) examining the effects of drinking black and green tea on lipids and blood pressure showed only modest, non-significant benefits.

The study also had limitations, including self-reported tea consumption and the possibility that other dietary and lifestyle factors influenced the results.

“Overall, tea seems to, maybe, have some cardiovascular benefits without a significant risk, so I favor tea consumption,” he said.

Michelle Routhenstein, a preventive cardiology dietitian at Entirely Nourished who was not involved in the research, emphasized that the findings do not establish a cause-and-effect relationship between drinking tea and a lower risk of vascular disease.

“Tea can be a helpful addition to a heart-healthy lifestyle, but it is not a substitute for addressing individual cardiovascular risk factors,” she said.

The researchers also found that drinking “burning hot” tea increased the risk of vascular disease by 16%, consistent with previous research raising concerns about the consumption of very hot beverages.

“I recommend enjoying your tea’s potential benefits by letting it cool to a comfortable sipping temperature before you drink it,” remarked Routhenstein.

The study examined black, green, Oolong, and other tea types.

The researchers found that black tea showed a more consistent association with a lower risk of vascular disease, which is contrary to some earlier research. However, they noted that these results don’t establish black tea as superior to green tea, and they don’t mean you should switch tea types.

“Both black and green tea are great choices for your heart health, and neither is definitively better than the other,” remarked Routhenstein.

“I recommend choosing whichever you enjoy and consuming it consistently, ideally without much added sugar,” Routhenstein noted.

Blumfield also noted that adding sugar or non-sugar sweeteners may change the potential health effects of drinking tea, so the findings should not automatically be extended to sweetened tea beverages.

Some older research suggests there may be additional health benefits to drinking both black and green tea. These benefits may include:.

Routhenstein said that tea may also support focus and alertness, improve hydration status, and potentially play a role in metabolic health.

“Enjoying tea can be a simple way to incorporate beneficial plant compounds into your day,” she added.

While drinking tea has been considered a health-promoting habit since ancient times, more research is needed to confirm its various health benefits.

What Does It Mean to Believe in God?

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (994 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Psychologytoday

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Posted November 16, 2026 | Reviewed by Abigail Fagan.
  • In his Ethics, Aristotle says that we should seek to understand each thing according to the kind of account it permits.
  • In a recent development, if we are adding or subtracting single-digit numbers, we can reasonably expect a reliable answer from a third grader.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Posted November 16, 2026 | Reviewed by Abigail Fagan.

In his Ethics, Aristotle says that we should seek to understand each thing according to the kind of account it permits. In solving an arithmetic problem, for example, we should expect an answer that is both accurate and precise. In the moral life, by contrast, we should seek an account that accords with what a practically wise person would have to say.

In a recent development, if we are adding or subtracting single-digit numbers, we can reasonably expect a reliable answer from a third grader. If, however, we are talking about friendship, marriage, or the relationship between a parent and offspring, we should turn elsewhere for insight, perhaps to the works of George Eliot or Leo Tolstoy.

A similar shift in expectation is appropriate when we think about belief in God. If God were a phenomenon susceptible to the sort of reasoning that we find in an arithmetic problem or a proof in symbolic logic, then it should be relatively easy to construct a knock-down argument for the existence and nature of God.

If, however, God is not quantifiable, then arithmetical approaches are not likely to serve us well, and if God is not like the major or minor premises of a syllogism (such as: All things we can conceive of exist; we can conceive of God; therefore, God exists), then we should not expect to “solve” God like a proof.

Industry observers note that likewise, if God is not made of matter, we should not expect to be able to reproduce the divine presence through scientific means, whether physical or chemical. The mere fact that God does not have mass, dimension, shape, location, or color does not establish that God is nothing more than a figment of human imagination.

Industry observers note that after all, we believe in numbers, although they lack all the physical properties just mentioned, and we also believe in love, justice, beauty, and truth, although they too cannot be counted, logically proved, or reproduced in a laboratory flask. There are things we believe to be real that we cannot see with our eyes or touch with our hands.

Industry observers note that if sacred texts are any guide, the best means we have of accounting for God are not the methods of mathematics, logic, or science, but those more closely aligned with literature or narrative. The Bible, for example, is full of stories, and while a few of these stories include God directly, many more address the effects of God’s presence in the unfolding of the human story.

It has been revealed that in one well-known metaphor, God is not something we directly apprehend, but we can sense God at work in the world much as we see and hear the breeze rustling the leaves on a tree. When Moses first senses God’s presence, it is in the form of a bush that is burning but not consumed by the flames, something only he has the curiosity and patience to see.

At this point, a skeptic might ask, If God is real, is it too much to ask that the divine should simply appear before us, work a few miracles, and thereby remove all doubt? But what if the problem is not God’s but ours? What if God cannot be put into any humanly constructed box because the divine is far beyond our meager intellectual and imaginative capacities?

What if we are talking about a reality that undergirds all of reality, not only as we know it but also far beyond our capacity to comprehend? What if we are seeking not just a clockmaker who set things in motion billions of years ago but a creator who sustains the universe from moment to moment as it continues to unfold even now in space and time?

Even the physical universe is far beyond our capacity to keep tabs on. A mature human organism consists of about 40 trillion cells, each one of which performs about 1 billion chemical reactions per second, which in turn requires the presence of about 100 trillion atoms of hydrogen. Of course, these are just round numbers – only God knows for sure.

Recent findings suggest that it is quite possible, perhaps likely, and based on past experience, all but certain that there is a great deal that we do not yet know about even the physical universe. It was only in 1895 that we first learned of the existence of x-rays and only in 1962 that we verified extra-terrestrial x-ray sources. What else still awaits our discovery?

Yet even to say that we still have a great deal more to discover hardly captures the full extent of the problem. For one thing, there may be more out there and in here, even if it is susceptible to our awareness or understanding, than we will ever uncover. And it is also possible that the greater part of it does not conform to our ways of knowing.

Perhaps being itself, as well as its source and end, is not an entirely anthropomorphic thing, in the sense that it is not built for our minds. It may have many other purposes far beyond us. And yet, here we are, blessed with the ability to perceive and understand some truly remarkable things, even if we can’t begin to get our hands around the whole thing.

Perhaps when it comes to God, poetry, music, art, and narrative are the best we can hope for – intimations, always allusive and never definitive. And yet, even here, we find truth and beauty for which we have every reason to be deeply thankful, for perhaps it is above all when we sense God’s presence, maybe with the aid of Eliot and Tolstoy, that we come most fully to life.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that in 1964, then-Pontiac division president John Z. Delorean (yes, that Delorean, of Back to the Future movie car fame) invented the muscle car category by bolting the significant-block V8 engine from the tech giant’s full-size cars into its lighter intermediate-sized chassis to create the legendary Pontiac GTO.

Recent findings suggest that kawasaki has done the same thing for its Jet Skis for the 2027 model year by installing the 310-horsepower supercharged 1.5-liter engine from its bigger Ultra models into the sporty, agile Jet Ski STX hull. The result is a truly eye-opening performance with what the manufacturer claims is its quickest Jet Ski yet.

Kawasaki established the personal watercraft industry with the 1973 introduction of the 27-horsepower JS400 Jet Ski. Since that time, however, the one-time industry leader has slipped in popularity compared to its rivals in the market.

Sources indicate that the tech giant’s 2027 plan to recapture customers includes an embrace of high performance. Kawasaki has rolled out five upcoming models for 2027, but the stars of the show are the high-performance Jet Skis meant to excite customers.

Sources indicate that the original Jet Ski employed a smokey 400 cc 2-stroke engine that grew to 800 cc over time. Those early Jet Skis were tricky stand-up models that delivered responsive handling but presented a learning curve that saw newcomers falling off repeatedly as they learned to master the machine.

Recent findings suggest that the solution was the introduction of the more stable sit-down models that traded responsiveness for stability. It was a trade that so many riders were willing to make that eventually Kawasaki phased out the stand-up models entirely.

Recent findings suggest that the industry shifted to cleaner 4-stroke engines in the ‘90s, and 1999 saw the arrival of the 1.5-liter engine based on Kawasaki’s sport motorcycle powerplants in its Jet Skis, packing 150 horsepower. In 2007, the engineering team bolted a supercharger to the same engine, producing 250 horsepower.

Sources indicate that now, thanks to the technology of Eaton’s Twin Vortices System supercharger design (which debuted on the 2009 Chevrolet Corvette ZR1), power has reached 310 horsepower. Packed into the agile STX sit-down hull to create the STX 310 model, the big motor lets riders rip across the water at 65 mph.

This drivetrain employs a 4-into-2-into-1 exhaust with dual water mufflers to minimize backpressure, maximizing the engine’s power and efficiency. The 160-mm jet pump has a three-blade impeller whose blade angles are optimized for peak acceleration and thrust.

It has been revealed that kawasaki let us ride the top-of-the-line STX 310RX, which lists for $20,199. There is a slightly less-well-equipped STX 310R that goes just as fast for $18,799. The test unit featured a 7-inch display panel containing the speedometer, tachometer, supercharger boost level, fuel level, trim setting, power mode setting, and compass. The rear-view camera on the STX lets the rider keep an eye on skiers, wakeboarders, or tube riders behind the watercraft.

We’ve gotten familiar with electronically controlled modes in modern cars, trucks, and motorcycles, and they are also present here in the Jet Ski STX 310RX. They are Smart Learning Operation (SLO), Lower Power Operation (LPO), Middle Power Operation (MPO), and Full Power Operation (FPO).

I started riding in MPO, thinking that would be a good get-acquainted scenario and I was pleasantly surprised at the STX 310’s speed. I guess I shouldn’t have been, considering that it has 310 horsepower. After a bit of that, I switched to FPO, and found the throttle response much touchier and acceleration quicker–perfect for significant fun.

MPO limits peak power to 80 percent, while FPO unleashes all 310 horses. LPO makes the throttle response even more sluggish and further restricts maximum power to 60 percent. SLO mode requires a special yellow key and is aimed at true beginners, who, realistically, probably should be learning on something other than this supercharged beast.

Industry observers note that other gadgets include the Launch Control system, which automatically adjusts the jet pump’s trim over the course of an acceleration run, keeping it optimized as the boat’s attitude changes during the run. There’s also a handy one-touch 5-mph cruise control, good for complying with no-wake zones.

According to recent reports, hot-dogging on the STX is a good time, thanks to a hull design that was created for corner carving, without much risk of pitching the rider into orbit mid-corner. There are also some nice practical features, like a Neutral that preserves some degree of steering capability.

Jet Skis have no rudder, relying on thrust from the engine to steer them, so when the throttle is released, or the boat is shifted to neutral, you’d expect it to be adrift. But Kawasaki employs a thrust reverser that lets the STX simultaneously have no forward thrust while also having some steering capacity. That reverser also provides for a Reverse position that lets the ride back the STX.

Reverse is one of the amenities that led to the demise of original-style stand-up Jet Skis, which aren’t suited to such features. Kawasaki tried briefly to revive the format in 2017, but states that its new stand-up 2027 models are Back to the Future to stay this time.

I was pleasantly surprised to find that long-dormant stand-up riding skills were still sufficient for me to take off on the first try without falling.

Recent findings suggest that kawasaki offers two versions of its classic stand-up model for 2027, the Jet Ski SX-R 160 and SX-X 160. These are powered by 160-hp naturally aspirated versions of the 1.5-liter engine, with the difference between them being that the SX-R has a traditional-style moveable handlebar that starts off lying flat and the rider lifts it as they stand.

The SX-X has a fixed motorcross-style handlebar, giving riders a choice between the two styles. The test model was the SX-X motocrosser. I’d never ridden one like that before, but I found the fixed bar seemed to make it easier to pull myself up as the ski got underway.

However, after falling off, as one does on these things, you have to reach up from the water to reattach your wrist lanyard to the ignition interlock. This is the thing that shuts the ski off when you fall so that it doesn’t leave you behind, and you have to reconnect it to restart the machine.

Recent findings suggest that but with the fixed bar up there pretty high from the water, I was happy to have my 35-inch sleeve length. Someone with more normal-length arms might find it hard to reach the switch while floating in the water alongside.

According to recent reports, just as I’d remembered stand-ups, the SX model is tremendously agile and fun for turns and jumps. And just as I remembered, it is easy to fall off in the process. Once it starts to roll onto its side, adding power might get you to ride out of it, or, as in my case, it might just make you hit the water while going even faster!

It has been revealed that it doesn’t matter which handlebar style you prefer because both the SX-X 160 and SX-R 160 are $11,999. Getting one of these would allow you to cultivate some old-school riding skills while taking advantage of some throwback value. That was another key component of the original Pontiac GTO’s muscle car legend, so it is good to see in the Kawasaki showrooms for 2027.

  • Short-tailed albatrosses (called makalena in Hawaiian) are almost completely white and feature a large pink bill.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Midway Atoll National Wildlife Refuge near Hawaii has welcomed a special couple: George and Geraldine, two short-tailed albatrosses (Phoebastria albatrus). The birds have officially found each other for nesting season on the Midway Atoll for the 10th straight year in a row. George was first spotted on October 18, and the pair was reunited by October 22.

It has been revealed that every fall, the remote group of islands becomes a temporary home to the world’s largest albatross colony. Albatrosses are a group of large migratory seabird species, including the wandering albatross (Diomedea exulans), which has the largest wingspan of any current bird species. One Laysan albatross (Phoebastria immutabilis), on the other hand, claims the title of oldest known banded wild bird—the famous Wisdom, who is over 70 years old.

Short-tailed albatrosses (called makalena in Hawaiian) are almost completely white and feature a large pink bill. They can live up to 50 years, and as exemplified by George and Geraldine, are monogamous. They nest on islands and atolls, and the species is listed as endangered by both the United States government and the state of Hawaii. At the turn of the 20th century, feather hunting almost made the species go extinct.

According to recent reports, “The vast majority of breeding for short-tailed albatross occurs on remote islands in the western Pacific, including Torishima Island, Japan, which is an active volcano south of Tokyo, and the Senkaku Islands near Taiwan,” according to the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service (FWS). “Since 2000, biologists at the [Midway Atoll National Wildlife] refuge have used short-tailed albatross decoys and audio playback of the seabird’s calls to attract more of them.”.

Industry observers note that in fact, George and Geraldine are the only breeding pair of short-tailed albatross on the Midway Atoll, though other members of their species were spotted last season. They were banded as chicks on Torishima Island and first seen together on Midway Atoll National Wildlife Refuge in 2016. The cute pair brought their first chick into the world during the 2018-2019 breeding season.

Industry observers note that “Millions of makalena once used their long wingspans to expertly glide on air currents across the northern Pacific Ocean, from Japan to Alaska and Hawaiʻi,” the FWS writes. “The slowly growing population is estimated at around 10,000 today.”.

Drug-Resistant ‘Superbugs’ Linked to More Than 50,000 Deaths a Year, CDC Says

📅 28 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (903 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Healthline

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Latest data show a substantial nationwide increase in potentially deadly infections caused by drug-resistant pathogens.
  • It has been revealed that the updated Antimicrobial Resistance (AR) Threats Report from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) states that drug-resistant bacteria and fungi cause approximately 9.7 million infections in the United States each year.
  • The estimated deaths in the United States from these drug-resistant pathogens have also risen from 35,000 to 50,800.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Latest data show a substantial nationwide increase in potentially deadly infections caused by drug-resistant pathogens.

It has been revealed that the updated Antimicrobial Resistance (AR) Threats Report from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) states that drug-resistant bacteria and fungi cause approximately 9.7 million infections in the United States each year. This is up from 2.8 million in a similar report from 2019.

The estimated deaths in the United States from these drug-resistant pathogens have also risen from 35,000 to 50,800.

According to recent reports, the new report also noted that infections that commonly occur in people in the hospital account for more than 42,000 deaths and cost the U.S. healthcare system more than $12 billion.

These findings are based on 2023 data. Officials from the CDC noted that the increase in drug-resistant infections from 2019 partially reflects a real rise in infections caused by certain resistant bacteria and fungi. However, they also noted that data sources and methodologies have changed, and direct comparisons between the two reports shouldn’t be made.

“These numbers are alarming by any measure but are particularly sobering when infectious diseases physicians connect real patients with these statistics in their everyday experience,” Wendy Armstrong, MD, President of the Infectious Diseases Society of America (IDSA), mentioned in a statement.

The CDC report highlighted 19 drug-resistant pathogens responsible for the 9.7 million annual infections. Four of these pathogens are classified as urgent threats, 13 as serious threats, and 2 as concerning.

The CDC also maintains a watch list that currently includes six pathogens.

The four pathogens classified as urgent threats are:.

William Schaffner, MD, a professor of the Division of Infectious Diseases at Vanderbilt University Medical Center, told Healthline that the reason for this increase in superbugs is, “Overuse of antibiotics; using them for too long or in circumstances where they do not offer a benefit.”.

“An example of the latter is the antibiotic treatment of common viral respiratory infections — antibiotics have no effect on viral infections. The widespread use of antibiotics kills off those bacteria that are susceptible to antibiotics, but then can leave a few bacterial survivors that are resistant to the effect of the antibiotics, resulting in the spread of these resistant strains,” he said.

Monica Gandhi, MD, a professor of medicine at the University of California, San Francisco, agreed and added, “This widespread use leads to selective drug pressure on the pathogen to evolve resistance to these antibiotics, making them harder to treat.”.

Industry observers note that “The risk to public health from these bugs is substantial. In fact, the World Health Organization (WHO) estimates up to 5 million deaths from these bugs worldwide every year, making these a substantial public health threat,” said Gandhi.

Candida auris tops the list of urgent threats.

Cases have increased nearly tenfold since the first detection in hospitals 10 years ago. This includes a more than 50% jump between 2022 and 2023.

Candida auris is a fungus that is almost completely resistant to one class of antifungal medications. It has also shown emerging resistance to the other two classes.

This fungus is often found on people’s skin, spreads rapidly in healthcare settings like hospitals, and affects some of the most vulnerable individuals.

Industry observers note that CRE is a family of multidrug-resistant bacterial pathogens. They have become increasingly difficult to treat and can share resistance with other bacteria.

These bacteria also pose a significant threat to people in hospitals, especially those with devices such as ventilators and catheters. A recent study found that CRE cases at U.S. hospitals increased by 18% between 2019 and 2023.

Industry observers note that while those in hospitals are especially vulnerable to CRE, 67% of the cases in 2023 were in the community. However, some of these cases may have occurred in people with recent exposure to healthcare.

Neisseria gonorrhoeae is the bacterium that causes gonorrhea, which is one of the most common sexually transmitted infections.

The CDC report noted that only a few antibiotics can effectively treat this infection.

Without effective treatment, gonorrhea can lead to:.

There are ways you can help prevent these superbugs:.

“[One] way individuals can help prevent the evolution of these superbugs is to not ask for antibiotics from their providers or urgent care settings in the setting of a viral infection,” noted Gandhi.

Experts and organizations like the CDC are working together to find ways to reduce the spread of these superbugs.

“Professional organizations and hospitals are educating their doctors and staff about the antibiotic resistance problem and have created reviews of practice patterns to encourage the appropriate use of antibiotics,” said Schaffner.

Gandhi added that organizations should institute procedures, such as “antimicrobial stewardship programs,” to ensure that providers do not prescribe antibiotics for non-bacterial infections and narrow antibiotics as soon as possible.

The Pioneering Antimicrobial Subscriptions to End Upsurging Resistance (PASTEUR) Act aims to revitalize antibiotic and antifungal development by changing the way the federal government pays for novel antimicrobials.

This act was reintroduced in Congress in February and is right now under review.

The focus on reducing the spread of superbugs and developing latest antibiotics is important.

“You really cannot have all the benefits of modern medicine, even outside the realm of infectious diseases, without effective antibiotics. It all goes away,” Haley Ann Pritchard, MD, medical director of infection prevention and antimicrobial stewardship at Eskenazi Health Hospital, said in a statement.

Musk admits Tesla doesn’t have enough talent to build more than one car at a time after exodus

📅 09 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1743 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Electrek

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that elon Musk now states Tesla can’t build the Cybertruck and the Cybercab at the same time because there are only so many “smart, dedicated people” to go around.
  • It’s the most honest explanation yet for how Tesla went from five consumer vehicle programs at the start of 2026 to a single platform, Model 3 and Model Y, by the middle of 2027.
  • On Friday, Musk stated Tesla would wind down Cybertruck production at Giga Texas around the middle of next year “to make room for increased Cybercab production.” As we pointed out at the time, Giga Texas isn’t short on space.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that elon Musk now states Tesla can’t build the Cybertruck and the Cybercab at the same time because there are only so many “smart, dedicated people” to go around. Half the executives he showed off in 2023 as proof of Tesla’s “bench strength” have since left the firm.

It’s the most honest explanation yet for how Tesla went from five consumer vehicle programs at the start of 2026 to a single platform, Model 3 and Model Y, by the middle of 2027.

On Friday, Musk stated Tesla would wind down Cybertruck production at Giga Texas around the middle of next year “to make room for increased Cybercab production.” As we pointed out at the time, Giga Texas isn’t short on space. The Cybertruck line runs at a fraction of its installed capacity because the truck sells a fraction of what Tesla planned.

A day later, replying to a user on X, Musk gave a different reason:.

It has been revealed that “The biggest thing most people fail to understand is that there are a very limited number of smart, dedicated people! They can only do so many things.”.

He added that if Tesla has to “maintain a complex production line, supply chain and allocate engineering for Cybertruck, we can’t use those people” for scaling Cybercab.

Industry observers note that by this morning, the explanation had shifted again, to the “opportunity cost of the complexity of Cybertruck.” But the Saturday version is the one that matters. Musk is telling us the bottleneck at Tesla isn’t factory space or money. It’s people.

The Cybertruck is the second casualty this year. In January, Musk confirmed the end of the Model S and Model X on Tesla’s Q4 earnings call and summed up the reason in one word: “Autonomy.” The Fremont line is being converted to build Optimus robots, and by April, only inventory was left.

The flagships had been on life support for years. Their last real enhancement was the 2021 interior refresh. The June 2025 “refresh” brought a upcoming paint color, a front bumper camera, a bit more range, and a $5,000 price increase. That’s not how you treat a vehicle program you care about.

According to recent reports, tesla painted a very different picture just two years ago. At its 2024 shareholder meeting, it showed this slide of its lineup: the Model 3, Model Y, Model S, Model X, Cybertruck, and Semi, plus three vehicles under covers that Musk stated were “going to be pretty special.”.

Of the five consumer vehicles on that slide, three are now dead or on their way out.

It has been revealed that so here’s what will be left in the second half of 2027: Model 3 and Model Y, two vehicles built on the same platform, plus the Model Y L and cheaper “Standard” variants of both. The Semi is a commercial truck. The Roadster’s production is still a giant question mark. And the Cybercab is a robotaxi with no steering wheel, not a car you can buy – even though Tesla is going to let fleet buyers get them to add on its own Robotaxi network. We previously explained how this is a terrible idea.

According to recent reports, for comparison, Hyundai Motor Group sells more than half a dozen EV models in the US across its Hyundai, Kia, and Genesis brands, on top of its gas and hybrid lineup. GM and Toyota run dozens of nameplates at once. Tesla can’t keep more than two programs alive at the same time.

Recent findings suggest that at Tesla’s Investor Day at Giga Texas on March 1, 2023, Musk mostly stayed out of the spotlight. Instead, Tesla paraded more than a dozen executives on stage to present its plans, a rare move for a company long criticized for being a one-man show.

“We’ve obviously got significant bench strength here,” Musk remarked at the time.

Of the 14 executives named as presenters that day, seven are gone:.

Martin Viecha, who ran investor relations through that event, left in April 2024 as well.

Seven are still at Tesla, according to their LinkedIn profiles: Tom Zhu, Lars Moravy, Franz von Holzhausen, Ashok Elluswamy, Karn Budhiraj, Laurie Shelby, and Brandon Ehrhart. And the ones who left weren’t peripheral. They ran batteries, powertrain, software, chips, energy, charging, and the money.

The bigger problem for Tesla’s ability to run vehicle programs is the program-level talent, the people who take a car from prototype to volume production.

Recent findings suggest that in November 2025, Tesla lost the head of its Cybertruck program, Siddhant Awasthi, and the Model Y program manager, Emmanuel Lamacchia, within a day of each other. Lamacchia had led Tesla’s best-selling vehicle for four years.

Then the Cybercab, the program Musk is now pulling people toward, started losing its own leaders:.

Add 17-year finance VP Sendil Palani and Thomas Dmytryk, the director who built Tesla’s over-the-air update system and Robotaxi infrastructure, both in March, and you get the picture.

So when Musk claims he needs Cybertruck’s people for Cybercab, part of the reason is that Cybercab keeps losing its own.

Recent findings suggest that musk will frame all of this as focus. Autonomy is going to be so big, the argument goes, that Tesla has to go all in.

It has been revealed that but we’ve heard that before. Tesla made the yoke steering wheel standard on the Model S and Model X in 2021 because the cars would soon drive themselves, then brought back a round wheel as an option. It removed the turn signal stalk from the Model 3 in 2023, then brought the stalk back in 2025 and started selling a $350 retrofit to owners. Each time, the autonomy that justified the change wasn’t there yet.

And Tesla isn’t the leader in unsupervised driving. It has the best driver-assist system on the market, but Waymo still logs roughly seven times more driverless miles per week, and NHTSA estimates Tesla’s entire Robotaxi fleet at about 1,000 vehicles. Zoox is scaling too, and Baidu’s Apollo Go runs a far bigger driverless fleet in China.

This is something that I’ve been highlighting for a decade. Even after it became a massive tech giant with a large headcount, Tesla has never been good at running several vehicle programs in a healthy way. The Model S and Model X were starved for updates long before the talent exodus started. Tesla has always thrown everything at its newest program and let the older ones coast.

Sources indicate that what changed is that the slack is gone. In 2023, Tesla could still neglect the flagships and keep them on the market, because it had deep benches in engineering, manufacturing, and software to absorb mistakes. Today, half the executives Musk called his bench are gone, and the people running the Cybercab ramp keep walking out. Musk is now openly telling us there aren’t enough people left to build a pickup truck and a robotaxi at the same time.

Musk calls it focus. It looks a lot more like a constraint Tesla can’t hire its way out of.

Tesla never had the capacity to hire, organize, manage and retain the amount of human talent required to develop multiple car model lines in concert. Tesla barely paid its staff enough for one model line development.

Recent findings suggest that you only need to look at other companies with decades of experience in developing many, separate (but technically strongly overlapping) model lines to see how much does that require in terms of human resources and in terms of R&D cost. Like BMW has always been investing ~5 billion EUR every year in R&D. That is how you have ~14 core models with at least another dozen specialist models and more regional models plus Mini and RR on top. At times up to 60 different significant variants with different drivetrains also impacting design, logistics and production. All being always in development for the next generation and also for a mid-life refresh or two. Across the whole group, including maintenance work, there can easily be triple-digit number of vehicle model projects going at the same time.

And Tesla can not even manage a handful.

Industry observers note that will the Cybercab be revolutionary and make it all worth it? We have our doubts. Tesla leads in driver assistance with FSD, but it has failed to evolve the product into unsupervised self-driving at scale, which it promised to buyers for a decade. It’s clearly not the leader in unsupervised self-driving, and the competition is crowded. Tesla’s lasting impact on the robotaxi market is genuinely hard to predict.

What’s not hard to see is the trend. Tesla has shown a complete inability to sustain multiple vehicle programs at once, and it’s getting harder for the automaker, not easier. If Tesla can’t hold on to the people who build its cars, how long before the Model 3 and Model Y get the same treatment as the Model S?

Both vehicle programs will undoubtedly go down in history as some of the most critical EVs of all time, but that doesn’t guarantee lasting success in a rapidly changing auto landscape.

Voyager 1 is almost one light-day away from Earth

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that voyager 1, the NASA space probe that has traveled farther from Earth than any other human-made object, is closing in on a remarkable milestone. Actually, let’s call it a 16.09-billion-milestone. That’s the distance a photon can travel in a single day, which is to say the Voyager 1 spacecraft will be exactly one light-day away from our planet on November 18 at 5:18 a.m. EST.

According to recent reports, at that moment, a radio signal sent from Earth would take 24 hours to reach Voyager 1, and then it would take another 24 hours for the probe’s response to come back. Imagine on a Friday morning telling your oven to turn on, but you don’t receive confirmation that it’s hot until Sunday. And by that point, the oven would have been baking whatever was inside for most of Saturday. That is the kind of delay that NASA’s Voyager team must work with.

Communicating with a machine at this superlative distance is “a pretty incredible endeavor,” Princeton University research scientist and heliophysicist Jamie S. Rankin tells Popular Science. Rankin is also a deputy project scientist of the Voyager mission. “In my mind the fun is receiving a signal back from the Voyager, a light-day away.”.

Rankin and other astronomers use those signals to study the very local interstellar medium, which is the suburb of space surrounding our solar system. Voyager 1 has been in this region, about 11 billion miles away, since 2012. There, the probe can detect changes in plasma and the magnetic field.

“Right now we’re trying to figure out how far out are the influences of the sun felt,” she indicates.

The sun continuously spits out charged particles in a stream of solar wind that extends into space. That wind pushes back against the gas and other interstellar stuff surrounding our solar system, sculpting a bubble in space known as the heliosphere. “There will be some part farther out, some distance away [where the] interstellar medium has no idea that the heliosphere is even there,” she states. Rankin adds that she thinks Voyager 1 is right on the edge of this “undisturbed, pristine interstellar medium.”.

In a recent development, it is something of a marvel that the almost 50-year-old Voyager 1 continues to supply astronomers with data. To send information to Earth, the probe uses a 23-watt radio transmitter (about the output of a small refrigerator lightbulb). Only antennas as sensitive as the 70-meter-wide dishes in the NASA Deep Space Network can detect Voyager 1’s super-faint signal. Without them, the space probe would have gone incommunicado years ago.

Industry observers note that when Voyager 1 rolled out in September 1977, the nuclear-powered spacecraft had 10 operational scientific instruments. It discovered new moons orbiting Jupiter and Saturn on its way out of our solar system; its observations of Jupiter’s moon Europa hinted at a liquid ocean under an icy crust. When the probe traveled beyond our solar system’s planets, NASA’s Voyager team shut down unnecessary equipment to conserve power. Now only two of its instruments are active. Ongoing management continues to preserve as much juice as possible from the spacecraft’s dwindling plutonium supply. The team was also forced to turn off the Low-energy Charged Particles experiment in April. In September, NASA swapped out three systems for lower-power alternatives on the Voyager 1, about six weeks after the same strategy worked on its twin Voyager 2 probe.

According to recent reports, “It’s fun to see what sort of innovation people come up with to keep the spacecraft going,” Rankin indicates. “There’s only so much you can turn off.”.

Voyagers 1 and 2 have been operating without several instrument heaters for years. If shutting those off hadn’t worked, Rankin claims “the mission would have ended a decade ago.”.

In a recent development, still, its operational margins are thin. In late October, NASA briefly lost contact with Voyager 1; that glitch has appeared to resolve itself and may have been related to a group of thrusters going offline.

According to recent reports, “This is the first time we’ve seen the spacecraft do something like this, but we are also at a point in the mission where we have to expect the unexpected,” Kareem Badaruddin, Voyager mission manager at NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL), remarked in a news release. “We’re relieved to be back in contact with Voyager 1 and are eager to understand what happened.” (JPL representatives did not respond to Popular Science’s requests for comment.).

All spacecraft missions must come to an end, no matter how plucky the probe or innovative its engineering team. NASA estimates that the Deep Space Network will lose contact with Voyager 1 around 2036, long before it travels to its two-light-day milestone. The probe may also freeze, unable to point properly back at Earth. Or its power systems will finally go kaput.

Industry observers note that “We know that’s coming at some point. It’s probably not 20 years from now,” Rankin says. “It’s probably not 10 years from now.”.

And then Voyager 1 will go forever radio silent as it cruises onward through the heavens.

Two Novel Solutions If You're Stuck in a Loneliness Trap

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Posted November 16, 2026 | Reviewed by Lybi Ma.

According to recent reports, though we understand that nostalgia is a powerful state—a sentimental longing for the past— we may fall short of harnessing it to transform our lives. A 2014 study published in Self and Identity found that experiencing nostalgia not only evokes positive emotions but also fosters personal growth. This growth is largely driven by positive self-regard, a key psychological resource, one that bolsters nostalgia.

Interestingly, the study also found that nostalgia strengthened feelings of belonging and provided a sense of meaning. These elements help counter loneliness. Here are two tips to make the most of your nostalgic reveries to counter feelings of loneliness and disconnection.

A prescient quote from the hit show The Office goes: “I wish there were a way to know you’re in ‘the good old days’ before you’ve actually left them.”.

The crucial insight is that people often don't recognize the value of experiences while living through them, but tend to view them more positively in retrospect. And this isn’t just anecdotal.

A classic study published in the Journal of Experimental Social Psychology explored how people anticipate, experience, and remember significant life events. Participants were divided into groups, each assigned to different events like vacations or trips. They were asked to anticipate these events, record their actual experiences during them, and then recall these experiences after some time had passed.

The study found that when participants recalled these events later, their memories were predominantly positive, more so than the actual experience. Negative aspects seemed to fade, leaving a “rosier” memory.

It has been revealed that once you embrace that you will long for your past, no matter how lonely it may seem now, you are more likely to create joyful experiences and memories. This can mean striking up a conversation with your barista, joining a volunteer group, or even a stroll in a park—you never know who you may run into.

Recent findings suggest that rosy retrospection empowers us to invest more in our daily interactions, not necessarily with grand expectations, but with an appreciation for their future value in our memories. The trick is recognizing the potential in ordinary moments to become extraordinary, nostalgic memories.

A recent study published in Emotion reveals how nostalgia can benefit individuals grappling with loneliness. The study found that for those who often feel a lack of direction or meaning in life—a common concern among the lonely—engaging in nostalgia can have a significant positive effect.

It has been revealed that this may be about recalibrating your sense of self in relation to the people around you. Think of it this way: Lonely individuals often feel like side characters in their own lives, often being overwhelmed by their isolation. Experiencing nostalgia (either spontaneous or self-induced) can help recenter their narrative, provided they contextualize the emotions and memories that are associated with the experience.

According to recent reports, if you’d like to contextualize and make the most of your nostalgia to regain a sense of meaning in your life, you can try the Hero’s Journey method. This approach involves effective storytelling, where you take charge of your life’s narrative through seven key steps:.

By mindfully engaging with nostalgia, you can weave a narrative that highlights your journey, underlines your growth, and reinforces your place within a larger community. This approach can combat loneliness and finding meaning.

Our memories are not just a source of comfort but also a bridge to a more fulfilling present. Nostalgia can be a powerful ally in easing loneliness, especially if you can look beyond the passive experience of it. Reflecting on positive past experiences can reframe how you view your current life situation. Generally, we remember the past as rosier than it was, which can help us appreciate the people in our lives more and foster better connections.

Fake rocks boost survival for venomous Australian snakes

📅 09 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (591 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Popsci

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Australia’s broad-headed snake (Hoplocephalus bungaroides) is as unique as it is threatened.
  • “Reintroducing any threatened species is challenging, especially when they’re captive bred,” explained University of Technology Sydney (UTS) wildlife ecologist Jonathan Webb.
  • Industry observers note that the broad-headed snake’s current predicament is the result of multiple issues.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Australia’s broad-headed snake (Hoplocephalus bungaroides) is as unique as it is threatened. However, ecologists at the University of Technology Sydney (UTS) have good news about this reptile. According to researchers, four of six captive-bred juveniles recently released into the Australian bush have survived their initial, most dangerous months outdoors. The team’s first-of-its-kind program may provide a promising path forward for the species—and a set of bespoke, artificial rocks may be the key.

“Reintroducing any threatened species is challenging, especially when they’re captive bred,” explained University of Technology Sydney (UTS) wildlife ecologist Jonathan Webb. “When the juvenile snakes are released, they risk getting eaten by either native predators, like kookaburras and brown snakes, or invasive predators such as cats or foxes.”.

Industry observers note that the broad-headed snake’s current predicament is the result of multiple issues. The distinct, yellow-banded serpent is slow to mature, and only begins reproducing around five years old. When it does, the nearly three-foot-long snake is one of the only venomous species known to give birth to live offspring. Although adults can live as long as 23 years in their native Sydney Basin, females only mate every two or three years. This leaves the broad-headed snake extremely susceptible to climate change, human impacts, and invasive predators. Any disruptions to the reproductive cycle can destabilize Australia’s population for generations—and the species has experienced plenty of disruptions over the last few decades.

“The broad-headed snake fascinated me because it used to be very common in the Sydney region, but even in the 1990’s it was quite rare,” said Webb. “Why was this species in trouble when other snake species were doing okay?”.

Recent findings suggest that webb noted that Australia’s increasingly frequent droughts and wildfires, coupled with habitat destruction, have made the broad-headed snake one the continent’s most threatened species. The intentional removal of bush-rocks for landscaping projects is also rough on the animals.Juveniles are particularly hard hit, as they rely on the bush-rocks for shelter and a steady diet of other reptiles like skinks and geckos.

“You can still buy rocks and boulders taken from the bush at your local landscape supplier, which is something I find really frustrating,” remarked Webb, adding that a single attractive boulder can sell for as much as $450. “That’s a pretty strong incentive for people.”.

According to recent reports, in collaboration with the conservation organization Aussie Ark and Indigenous representatives of the Traditional Owners of the Shoalhaven region, Webb’s team have bred eight broad-headed snakes in captivity since 2024. Biologists kept one pair of snakes for their genetics, then released the other six at restoration sites in May. However, the juveniles weren’t left stranded in the bush. Researchers placed them beneath custom artificial rocks designed with ideal crevice measurements to mirror natural geologic formations’ thermal properties. Webb noted the rocks were “critical” to the snakes’ survival odds.

“Broad-headed snakes are nocturnal so they shelter under these rocks during the day and rely on them for warmth, protection and to attract prey,” he explained.

Recent findings suggest that biologists hope to expand the program elsewhere in Australia, and breed even more broad-headed snakes for release. Although it’s a slow process, their early successes indicate a potentially ecosystem-altering solution for the reptiles.

“We now have a unique, multi-faceted, holistic program that’s a model for threatened species conservation Australia-wide, and I couldn’t be prouder of our team and our partners,” added Aussie Ark founder Tim Faulkner.

Ford’s EV batteries retain more than 90% health after 100,000 miles

  • The Mustang Mach-E went on sale in late 2020 as Ford’s first fully electric crossover SUV designed from the ground up.
