📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, your electric vehicle battery may last longer than you think. Ford claims its EV batteries retain greater than 90% health on average after 100,000 miles. Here are a few tips to keep yours healthy.

The Mustang Mach-E went on sale in late 2020 as Ford’s first fully electric crossover SUV designed from the ground up.

Since launching the 2021 Mustang Mach-E, Ford has been collecting data from over 36,000 vehicles that have traveled two billion miles across the US and Canada.

According to Ford, the Mach-E’s battery has retained 92% of its health on average over the past five years.

Across its full EV lineup, including the F-150 Lightning and E-Transit, Ford remarked its battery packs maintain more than 90% health on average after 100,000 miles. The key number to look at is the spread, with 95% of vehicles falling between 87% and 97% health.

Of 2021 model-year EV owners, Ford stated, more than 2,000 have crossed 100,000 miles with their original battery averaging better than 91% health, while over 30 have crossed the 200,000-mile mark and average 88% health.

Ford is using real-world data to help owners take good care of their electric vehicles, no matter how much they know about batteries and other EV tech.

It’s also applying lessons from developing the Universal Electric Vehicle (UEV) platform, which will underpin its next-generation EVs, starting with the Fantom pickup next year.

In a recent development, ford offered a few simple, everyday tips to help owners support long-term battery health. For one, if possible, charge at home on Level 2 for daily commuting or driving and save DC fast charging for longer trips.

It also helps to avoid charging in extreme temperatures if you can. Preconditioning the battery can help bring it into the optimal temperature range, while parking in the shade on hot summer days can also help avoid long-term battery degradation.

Last, but not least, you can use the Ford App to find charge-level recommendations designed specifically for your vehicle and battery system.

The 2021 Mustang Mach-E uses an NCM battery, but some newer Ford batteries use a lithium iron phosphate (LFP) battery chemistry, which is recommended to charge to 100% from time to time.

Ford has introduced upcoming features in the Ford App to help owners maintain battery health specific to their vehicle and will continue to use the data to improve the experience as it introduces its next-gen EVs.

Now, I have no idea how this car has been used or charged since newly introduced (does have the DCFC since it's a 2017). And since it's range was 115 miles factory rated, I have no idea if it's been charged to 100% most or all of the time. What I can tell you is that when I charge it to 100% now, it's giving me about 120 miles on average and I've seen as high as 134 miles. If I turn the A/C on, those numbers drop to 110 on average. Since I live in a mild climate and use the A/C sparingly, my daily commute with mixed driving is giving me a real life 120 to 125 miles.

Not bad for a nearly 10 years old compliance EV!!

Ford will open pre-orders for the Fathom, a midsize electric pickup and first UEV-based model, starting at $28,350 in early 2027.

Meanwhile, the 2027 Ford Mustang Mach-E is now on sale, starting at $39,995. The 2027 Mach-E drops the standard-range battery offered in the 2026 model and now comes standard with the larger 88 kWh battery with an EPA-estimated range of up to 320 miles (RWD).

Latest Update: Bunny Williams Never Set Out to Collect Birdhouses—Now a Whole Village of Them Stands in Her Connecticut Garden

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that among the apple trees at the edge of AD100 Hall of Famer Bunny Williams’s storied country garden in Falls Village, Connecticut, stands a church with a sensible tin roof; a thatched cottage; a pagoda; a red house flying a tiny flag that she takes for a general store; and a shuttered confection that suggests a Russian dacha.

  • A farmhouse with a side porch crafted by the late Larry Smith, a North Georgia birdhouse builder known for fashioning charmingly detailed structures with metal roofs.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that among the apple trees at the edge of AD100 Hall of Famer Bunny Williams’s storied country garden in Falls Village, Connecticut, stands a church with a sensible tin roof; a thatched cottage; a pagoda; a red house flying a tiny flag that she takes for a general store; and a shuttered confection that suggests a Russian dacha. Each is raised high on its own post, finished on every side, painted and weathered like the structures of a settled town—and none has a door you could fit a hand through. It is a hamlet fashioned for birds, assembled building by building, the way real towns often grow: slowly, and without a master plan.

According to recent reports, for many years as Williams and her husband, the antiques dealer John Rosselli, combed fields and fairs for Treillage, the much-loved shop they ran in New York City until 2015, the birdhouses kept finding her. They gathered on shelves in the hayloft of her barn. “When I had two, I didn’t know what to do with them,” she states. “Then all of a sudden there were 10.” She decided they had been in storage long enough.

A farmhouse with a side porch crafted by the late Larry Smith, a North Georgia birdhouse builder known for fashioning charmingly detailed structures with metal roofs.

An A-frame house embellished with gingerbread trim and decorative brackets.

Williams, on a tree stump next to the pagoda. The notch in the base of the birdhouse indicates that it was probably designed to be mounted on a roof.

At that point, Williams and Robert Reimer, head gardener on her property, started the process of reclaiming a long-overlooked point of land. To create space and liberate a stand of existing apple trees, they removed invasive species, then planted oat grass, bird-friendly scrub plants, and fruit-bearing pawpaw trees. To create the neighborhood, she had uniform posts made—tall, “so that you look up at them,” each wrapped with a metal band to deter ambitious squirrels from climbing too high and disturbing the tenants she had in mind. Finally, up went the houses, now totaling 17.

Industry observers note that the attraction had nothing to do with value or pedigree. “Most of these birdhouses are sort of folk art,” she says. “They were somebody having fun building an unusual structure.” Not Monticello in miniature, not a replica of someone’s own house, just unknown makers, each with “an eye and a kind of humor,” none of them trying to be perfect. The proof is in the details: the gingerbread scallops on one many-holed high-rise (“somebody had a great time with their little saw”), the thatched-roof cottage she prizes because she has never seen another like it, the weather vane crowning the would-be dacha.

A church with a brick chimney, an oversized cupola, and Gothic Revival design elements.

A country church with a tin roof.

A rare combination house and feeder that evokes a neoclassical temple.

Williams calls this one the general store.

A colonial revival house with a columned portico built by Larry Smith.

“It has a kind of Russian dacha feeling,” states Williams.

What she didn’t have was history—the dealers who sold them seldom had any to pass along. The record, it turns out, is often recoverable. “The period from 1890 to 1930 is really the birdhouse’s golden age,” claims Jacob Torkelson, an architectural historian and researcher at the University of Pennsylvania’s Stuart Weitzman School of Design, and among the very few scholars in the country studying these objects, whose makers and manufacturers he has painstakingly been identifying, where a name survives. Across those decades, government pattern books encouraged farmers to install birdhouses to reduce pesticide use (the birds would eat the insects), while mail-order companies offered them to homeowners as pure whimsy, not to mention a way of promoting biodiversity in their gardens. Shown photographs of Williams’s collection, Torkelson supplied some of what the dealers couldn’t. He traced one house down to the catalog page: the six-room Bungalow Martin House sold by the E.F. Hodgson Company, which listed the model from about 1917 until the firm closed in 1944. “Birdhouses are these wonderful mirrors to the human condition,” Torkelson says. “They tell us the values that we have as a society or as individuals, in our houses, in our gardens.”.

A double porch house also built by Larry Smith.

This pagoda-inspired birdhouse provides multiple roosting spots.

An unusual thatched-roof cottage prized by Williams, who has never seen another like it.

Industry observers note that williams isn’t finished collecting. Last May at Trade Secrets, the annual Litchfield Hills garden fair she cofounded in 2001 to raise funds for a local nonprofit domestic violence support agency, she stopped at the tent of Jim Sidon, whose company, Sparrow 10:29, crafts avian-size replicas of real buildings. Sidon, based outside Atlanta, came to the work after retiring from the printing industry. His first architectural birdhouse, built in 2017, was a replica of the 1792 Federal-style mansion in Newburyport, Massachusetts, where he and his wife had rented two rooms as newlyweds. It was Sidon who recognized, in three of Williams’s houses, the hand of his late friend Larry Smith, a North Georgia birdhouse builder known for his metal roofs and charmingly rustic details. Williams has asked Sidon to build her something latest, though she is still deciding exactly what. Unlike her anonymous makers, Sidon numbers and signs every house. “My hope is that years from now, someone’s searching that out,” he says, “and when they open it up, they’ll see my signature.”.

A dovecote-inspired birdhouse offers multiple residences.

A picturesque house topped with a prominent weather vane.

Drawing the eye like miniature garden follies, the houses rise on poles amid a stand of apple trees from ground planted with oat grass and bird-friendly scrub plants.

In Falls Village, the upkeep routine is minimal: Every couple of years the houses come down, receive a coat of wood preservative, and go back up into the weather. Sidon’s constructions, with cedar exteriors and sealed against the elements, ask even less. His replica of the Newburyport house has stood in his own garden for nearly a decade untouched. “I just hose it off,” he states. None of this troubles Torkelson, a preservationist by training. “These houses were made to be ephemeral,” he says. “They weren’t made to last forever, and they should absolutely be used.”.

It has been revealed that as for the intended residents? Williams thinks the birds mostly prefer making their homes in the trees, where they carry on, she says, like a symphony orchestra: “I’ve always felt that one of the reasons they don’t live in these houses is the birds think it’s suburbia. But they like the atmosphere.” Come winter, when the woods go bare and the village shows through the branches, Sidon would bet the houses do get used, songbirds crowding in two and three at a time for warmth. Williams can’t say—she has never once climbed up to look. “If they are nesting,” she says, “I don’t want to bother them.”.

Taking Fish Oil to Boost Brain Health? A 2-Year Study Questions the Benefits

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, A clinical trial found that taking high dose omega-3 supplements for 2 years did not help memory or thinking skills in older adults at increased risk of Alzheimer’s.Researchers at Keck Medicine of USC led the study, which was published in eBioMedicine.
  • Getting omega-3s from food or supplements is important since the body cannot make them.
  • Keck Medicine researchers enrolled 365 adults who did not have dementia, and whose ages ranged from 55 to 80, with an average age of 66.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, A clinical trial found that taking high dose omega-3 supplements for 2 years did not help memory or thinking skills in older adults at increased risk of Alzheimer’s.Researchers at Keck Medicine of USC led the study, which was published in eBioMedicine. Participants took either a daily high dose supplement of omega-3 fatty acid docosahexaenoic acid (DHA) or a placebo.Fish oil is one of the most familiar ways people get omega-3s. However, the supplement in this clinical trial wasn’t made from fish, Hussein Yassine, MD, director of the USC Center for Personalized Brain Health with Keck Medicine of USC and the study’s lead researcher, told Healthline. This article uses the broader term omega-3 supplements.The researchers found that taking supplements raised omega-3 levels in participants’ brains, yet it didn’t change their memory, thinking skills, or brain structure.Dung Trinh, MD, an internist at MemorialCare Medical Group and chief medical officer of Healthy Brain Clinic in Irvine, California, who wasn’t involved in the study, told Healthline that the findings challenge the common belief that omega-3 supplements, such as fish oil, can help prevent Alzheimer’s disease or improve memory.Millions of older adults take omega-3 supplements. In a 2017–2018 federal survey, 21.8% of U.S. adults age 60 and older reported taking an omega-3 fatty acid supplement in the past 30 days, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC).

Getting omega-3s from food or supplements is important since the body cannot make them.

Keck Medicine researchers enrolled 365 adults who did not have dementia, and whose ages ranged from 55 to 80, with an average age of 66.

Subjects obtained little DHA from their diets and had at least one risk factor for dementia. Of the 365 people who enrolled, 225 completed the trial, according to the study. Nearly half (47%) carried APOE4.Participants took either 2,000 milligrams (mg) of DHA or a placebo every day. Neither participants nor researchers knew who received the supplement.

The supplement in the trial contained more than 90% DHA and about 1% EPA, Yassine noted.

Researchers found that high dose omega-3 supplements raised DHA levels in the fluid around the brain and spinal cord by 17%.

In a recent development, both groups in the trial scored about the same on memory and thinking tests. Brain structure appeared the same in both groups.

The supplement also raised omega-3 levels in the blood. Over two years, participants’ omega-3 index, a measure of EPA and DHA in red blood cells, rose from 4.9% to 11%.“That’s a massive increase, but that doesn’t translate into clinical outcomes,” Yassine mentioned.DHA reached the brain equally well in people with and without the gene variant APOE4, which is linked to a higher risk of Alzheimer’s disease, according to the study.Earlier trials couldn’t tell whether DHA failed to reach the brain or reached it without helping, the study’s authors say. This trial answers that open question, since the DHA got there.“This tells us that just because a supplement reaches the brain doesn’t necessarily mean it will improve brain function or prevent cognitive decline,” Trinh said.

According to recent reports, the lack of measurable change in memory and thinking may come down to how the body uses omega-3s, according to Yassine.He remarked it’s “really vital to distinguish between omega-3 metabolism and omega-3 supplements.”A supplement can raise omega-3 levels, yet the body may still break them down before they reach the right places. Obesity, smoking, and a lack of exercise can all reduce how much omega-3 gets into the brain, he said.

Some fish and fish oil supplements may offer more than omega-3s. These sources may also include other nutrients such as lutein, vitamin E, and selenium, Yassine remarked.A supplement can raise the level, but if you don’t change the holistic program, just going and increasing the level by itself may not be sufficient,” he said.Researchers tend to fall into two camps on how to read the results, according to Yassine.

Industry observers note that some see the findings as evidence that supplements don’t work in isolation. Others argue the trial would need a longer follow-up or sicker participants to answer the question.Trinh pointed to the study’s length. “It’s also notable to recognize that Alzheimer’s disease develops over decades, so a two-year study may not be long enough to determine whether DHA supplementation has any long-term preventive benefits,” he mentioned.

Fish oil supplements contain two omega-3 fatty acids, eicosapentaenoic acid (EPA) and DHA, according to the National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health (NCCIH).

Foods such as fish and flaxseed also contain omega-3s, according to the National Institutes of Health’s Office of Dietary Supplements (ODS).Research suggests omega-3s may help reduce inflammation, support heart health, and promote childhood growth and development.

Some observational studies link diets high in omega-3s with a lower risk of cognitive decline and dementia.

It has been revealed that researchers say omega-3s may help preserve cognition by supporting brain cells in continuing to function and maintain their membranes, according to the ODS.“Omega-3s are important for the brain, and we and many others have shown that having higher levels of omega-3s is associated with less Alzheimer’s pathology, better cognition, and many other protective outcomes,” Yassine stated, in contrast to the trial findings.Trinh agreed. “DHA plays an essential role in maintaining healthy brain cells, and there is evidence that eating fish as part of a healthy dietary pattern may support long-term brain health,” he said.Research on omega-3s and brain health is ongoing, and there is insufficient evidence to draw firm conclusions about their effectiveness.

Some people may still benefit from a supplement, according to Yassine, including:.

Some neurologists test omega-3 levels, though the test isn’t standard, Yassine stated.People with nutritional deficiencies or certain genetic or metabolic traits may respond differently to omega-3 supplements, and researchers still need to learn who might benefit, Trinh said.

People who already take fish oil or other omega-3 supplements for other reasons, such as high triglycerides, should make those decisions with their healthcare professionals, he stated.

Trinh mentioned he tells his patients that “what is good for the heart is generally good for the brain.” He recommended the following healthy habits:.

“Overall, this study reminds us that there is no magic pill for preventing Alzheimer’s disease and that maintaining brain health requires a much broader approach,” Trinh mentioned.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Tesla Cybertruck, as you may well have heard by now, is on death row. How the news hits you will likely depend on what your opinions on the truck that manufacturer CEO “Technoking” Elon Musk once described as “what Bladerunner would have driven.” Those who dislike the steel-bodied machine range from pleased to gloating; fans, meanwhile, are rending garments and clutching their vowel-less vanity plates. Alas, poor Cybertruck; I knew him, Elon!

Sources indicate that but one group of Tesla enthusiasts are aiming to take matters into their own hands. Unplugged Performance, an aftermarket shop specializing in Teslas, has taken to social media to entreat the automaker not to kill off the slab-sided pickup, but rather, to license its production out to them instead.

It has been revealed that the company took to X—which is owned by Musk, who is also, shall we say, a vocal user—to make the offer. “An open offer to Tesla: We fully support putting Cybercab first, and we’d be glad to take the Cybertruck line off your hands. We’d fund it with a consortium of investors and run it at no cost to Tesla’s floor space, headcount, or focus,” Unplugged Performance wrote.

That offer, unsurprisingly, evoked a reaction amongst Internet-active fans of the Cybertruck, as well as quite a few questions for specifics. To their credit, Unplugged Performance responded with a comprehensive amount of detail regarding the plan so far. “A fair question we’re hearing: can UP really run the Cybertruck vehicle line? Not alone, and not overnight,” the brand tweeted (X-ed?), before elaborating that it intends to round up investors and manufacturing partners in the months leading up to Tesla’s planned changeover of its Texas plant that will use the capacity currently occupied by the truck to build autonomous Cybercabs.

“We believe this is highly fundable because one production platform serves three markets: existing demand for the pickup, pent-up demand for a seven-seat SUV, and Robotaxi network vehicles in useful all-terrain form factors (seven-seat people movers, cargo haulers, and pickups),” Unplugged Performance continued.

“Should add,” the shop added, “the number of Tesla alumni who have reached out offering to help has been overwhelming. For anyone questioning talent or experience, we already have a strong and resourceful team, and many people who helped build these vehicles want to participate and see the platform live on.”.

As of this story’s Wednesday afternoon publication, Tesla and Musk don’t appear to have offered a public response to Unplugged’s offer. That said, Musk did post on Wednesday that pickup production is being extended through summer of next year to “work through more of the Cybertruck order backlog.” And given his follow-up, who knows? Maybe he’d be open to letting someone else take over after that.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Posted November 16, 2026 | Reviewed by Gary Drevitch.

Industry observers note that as a college professor for over 30 years, I have worked with countless students who either claim they hate reading or report that they've never finished an entire book. To succeed in college, it’s vital to read what’s assigned. It’s also important to read for pleasure. Why? Because, simply put, it makes you more interesting.

With students nearing the end of the semester and hopefully thinking about how they can improve their habits and skills for the latest semester, it is worth thinking about the role of reading. With the holiday break almost upon us, it's the perfect time to practice and to embark on a potentially interesting book.

In a recent development, people who read have a greater sense of fluency of ideas and perspectives that they can bring to bear on conversations, and they possess stronger vocabularies. These qualities give people an edge both socially and professionally. Referencing something you read and learned that resonates with you or naturally relates to a conversation during a job interview, for example, helps position you as someone with insight and depth.

The other thing to remember is that the habit of reading often translates to greater agility with writing. When you have more exposure to a variety of ways that ideas are expressed, you’re able to gather more information to craft what you want to say.

According to recent reports, college is a great time to discover exactly what it is that you like to read. This is especially true if you’re coming to college with little interest in reading. This lack of interest is often due to not having had much say in what you got to read in high school. So, now’s the time to think about what you gravitate to most. What do you find most moving and compelling? Maybe it’s fiction, nonfiction, creative nonfiction, or poetry. Whatever it is, reading is a passport for the experience of world-traveling, which is a gift you can give yourself.

According to recent reports, if your parents read to you when you were a child, they may have shown you the value and joy of reading. I’ve started directly asking my students if a parent or guardian read to or with them, what their favorite book was as a child, and what their favorite is now. What’s most sad for me is when students aren’t able to name a single book and instead tell me they “never read,” “never had a parent read to me,” “hate reading,” or “never finished a book.”.

But even if the value of reading was not instilled in you growing up, it’s not too late to develop a habit of reading for pleasure. Find something that potentially interests you, put your phone away where it’s not even visible, grab a fun drink or snack, and curl up in a cozy space and read. Try just 15 minutes at first. If you like it, keep going. If you find yourself restless or sleepy, try to push through a bit longer, and if that doesn’t work then go do something else and make a commitment to yourself to return to the book the next day. Typically, those in the regular practice of reading and enjoying it generally find it easier to be alone and enjoy solitude.

In summary, when college students work to strengthen their reading muscle, both in terms of reading for classes and for pleasure, they encounter the following benefits:.

Shadow’s potentially new partner Kaydee was also heard nearby and she landed on the nest.

Sources indicate that however, just after landing, Kaydee was on high alert because another eagle was eyeing the nest from above. Shadow quickly responded with loud vocals, and came swooping past the nest. While the intruding eagle briefly followed Shadow away, it made a turn back towards the nest. Kaydee made more calls to Shadow and quickly flew out of the nest, as the intruder tried to land on the branches above her. Shadow returned to the nest, and put himself between Kaydee and the intruder above, and all three birds flew away. Eventually, Shadow perched on a nearby tree and was heard giving a warning call in a loud voice while standing watch. The scene that appeared straight out of a movie was another exciting moment for the eagles of Major Bear Valley.

It has been revealed that “The brief encounter last night definitely revealed Shadow and Kaydee defending the nest, protecting it and each other,” writes Friends of Big Bear Valley (FOBBV), the non-profit organization that runs the livestream. “What a delight to see them as they have truly been missed these past two weeks!”.

According to FOBBV, Shadow is ALSO an “experienced master builder and knows exactly when it’s time to begin tidying up the nest, moving stick furniture or placing latest guardrails or a baby gate.”.

Recent findings suggest that we still do not know if Shadow and Kaydee will mate this season. Bald eagle nesting officially begins in September, and lasts over six months, depending on when the the chicks fledge. Eggs are typically laid in January. Viewers can follow Shadow and Kaydee and their journey on the nest via a 24/7 livestream.

Kaydee, formerly known as KD1, is a banded female bald eagle that has been spotted in Big Bear Valley following the death of Shadow’s former partner, Jackie. She was born in 2022, about 70 miles away from Big Bear Lake in the Prado Basin between Anaheim and Riverside, California. Coincidentally, her parents are also named Lucky and Ricky like Jackie’s parents, but they are a different eagle pair.

According to recent reports, kaydee was banded as part of the Orange County Water District’s work to track the eagles born in the area. These bands help biologists track and monitor the birds over time. Kaydee at the moment has a black spot on her head, but it may not be permanent. It’s possible that not all of her white feathers have come in or it could be tree sap or dirt. She also has two small bands on her legs. One is a small metal band, while the other is a lavender band with “KD1” on it.

Industry observers note that kaydee is almost five years old, so she is just about ready to mate. She was recently spotted on FOBBV’s livestream inspecting the nest and has also been seen hanging out near Shadow. Flying around Massive Bear is completely normal behavior for young adult eagles at this time of year.

In a recent development, in January, Jackie laid two eggs in the nest, but ravens destroyed them. She later laid two more eggs that hatched in April and named Luna and Sandy. The name Sandy is in honor of FOBBV’s former executive director Sandy Steers who died from cancer in February.

On July 17, Jackie was found injured on the ground near Dana Point Park, California. Cell phone video from a witness confirmed that she had an altercation with two other subadult eagles. She successfully fended off the other eagles by turning over and using her talons, but could not fly far away.

She was transferred to the Ojai Raptor Center for care, where she was diagnosed with severe anemia. Her anemia worsened during the first week of August, the Ojai Raptor Center said that she was in unstable condition on August 9. Her packed cell volume (PCV) fell below percent, before rising to nine percent. Jackie died early in the morning on August 10. The necropsy did not reveal a single cause of death, and instead pointed to several factors including severe anemia, bird flu, blood clots in her wing and one kidney, and liver and lung abnormalities.

In a recent development, A memorial service was held on September 5 in Fawnskin, California, along with a second celebration of life called Wings Over Major Bear on October 3. The event featured representatives from FOBBV, the Yuhaaviatam of San Manuel Nation, and more.

The electric Vespa just got better where it actually matters

📅 09 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (788 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Electrek

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that vespa’s electric scooters have never exactly screamed for attention.
  • But for 2027, Vespa has given its electric lineup a fairly significant technological overhaul while leaving that iconic steel bodywork largely untouched.
  • Recent findings suggest that unveiled at EICMA 2026 in Milan, the newly introduced electric Vespa lineup now consists of the Primavera Elettrica, Sprint S Elettrica, and the faster Primavera Tech Elettrica.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that vespa’s electric scooters have never exactly screamed for attention. That’s sort of the point. They look like Vespas, ride like Vespas, and just happen to swap the gasoline engine for a much quieter electric drivetrain.

But for 2027, Vespa has given its electric lineup a fairly significant technological overhaul while leaving that iconic steel bodywork largely untouched.

Recent findings suggest that unveiled at EICMA 2026 in Milan, the newly introduced electric Vespa lineup now consists of the Primavera Elettrica, Sprint S Elettrica, and the faster Primavera Tech Elettrica. And while you’d be forgiven for struggling to spot the differences from across the show floor, there’s a lot more happening underneath.

According to recent reports, the biggest upgrade is an entirely fresh electric motor developed and manufactured in Italy by Vespa parent company Piaggio Group. The motor uses a new modular design intended to improve both performance and efficiency, while also doing away with rare-earth materials.

Sources indicate that on the 45 km/h (28 mph) Primavera and Sprint S models, Vespa claims the upcoming motor provides stronger acceleration for stop-and-go city riding. Range reaches up to 85 km (53 miles) in Eco mode.

Sources indicate that but perhaps the biggest practical improvement is the upcoming removable battery. Being able to pull the battery out of the scooter and carry it inside for charging makes a massive difference for urban riders who don’t have access to a garage or dedicated charging spot – exactly the kind of riders Vespa is targeting.

Sources indicate that the Primavera Tech is where things get a little faster. This version is homologated as a motorcycle rather than a moped in Europe and reaches 67 km/h (42 mph). That’s still not terribly fast, but the electric Vespa line has never been known for its top speed.

Its range has increased by 12.5% thanks to the new motor and Vehicle Management System, reaching 90 km (56 miles) on the WMTC cycle or up to 100 km (62 miles) in Eco mode.

Sources indicate that there’s also a fresh charger that Vespa says reduces energy consumption from the wall by 17%, with a 0-80% charge taking around 2.5 hours. A new Maintenance mode is designed to protect the battery during longer periods when the scooter isn’t being ridden.

Sources indicate that vespa is clearly only really interested in selling their gas models, which come in 50cc, 125cc, & 310cc classes. And the only reason anyone would get a 50cc is if they didn't want to bother to get an actual motorcycle license in some jurisdictions. The electrics are nearly as expensive as the 310s but even the "faster" model only has the power equivalent of about 70cc's. At least the battery in the faster model is now a decent 4.2 kwh, though that one I believe is not removable. Hey I'm actually a Vespa lover I have a 200cc. They are beautiful quality machines, and I don't mind the price premium. But the electrics are quite disappointing, especially for the money. If they had a true 125cc equivalent I would be first in line at the showroom. Very disappointing in that a stouter motor really wouldn't cost them much more at all.

The Primavera Tech also gets the technological bells and whistles you’d expect from the flagship version, including a 5-inch TFT display, keyless operation, navigation through Vespa’s smartphone connectivity system, and remote seat unlocking.

Perhaps the most Vespa thing about the whole enhancement is how little of it you can actually see.

Industry observers note that the tech giant hasn’t tried to turn its electric scooters into rolling science-fiction props. They’re still unmistakably Vespas, complete with the same classic styling that has defined the brand for generations. They just happen to have a much more interesting electric drivetrain hiding underneath now.

Of course, they also carry some very Vespa pricing. While we don’t have word on the updated pricing for the newly introduced models, the outgoing Primavera Elettrica 70 RED was priced at $8,299 in the US. So don’t expect these models to come cheap.

Losing even one hour of sleep can make you more susceptible to scams

📅 09 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (530 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Popsci

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that A poor sleep schedule doesn’t only affect your overall mood, energy levels, and long-term health.
  • “Our results demonstrate that even though you may not be aware of it, lack of sleep leads to impulsive choices, and you may lose more than you gain from putting sleep on the back burner,” noted UC Irvine neurobiologist and study co-author Eitan Schechtman.
  • If you have already fallen prey to a scam email in the past, you can at least take some small comfort in the knowledge that you aren’t alone.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that A poor sleep schedule doesn’t only affect your overall mood, energy levels, and long-term health. Fresh evidence indicates that losing as little as one hour of rest may increase your chance of falling for an online scam by over 10 percent the following morning. Neurobiologists at the University of California, Irvine, laid out their findings in a study published today in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (PNAS), arguing that even minimal sleep disruptions can have almost immediate consequences.

“Our results demonstrate that even though you may not be aware of it, lack of sleep leads to impulsive choices, and you may lose more than you gain from putting sleep on the back burner,” noted UC Irvine neurobiologist and study co-author Eitan Schechtman.

If you have already fallen prey to a scam email in the past, you can at least take some small comfort in the knowledge that you aren’t alone. Cybercrimes continue to increase exponentially in the United States. The FBI’s Internet Crime Complaint Center received over one million reports in 2025—a nearly 25 percent increase from only five years earlier.

It has been revealed that remaining aware of con artist tactics and staying up-to-date on personal cybersecurity strategies are some of the best ways to protect yourself. However, Schechtman and his colleagues recently wondered if something as seemingly inconsequential as a single evening of bad sleep may also put people at risk for schemes like an email phishing attack. To investigate, the team partnered with a large, unnamed manufacturer as it ran a cybersecurity awareness campaign for more than 11,000 employees. Multiple times a year, the company’s IT department issued emails imitating phishing attempts, then tallied how many workers clicked through the fake malicious links. Schechtman’s team then analyzed results both before the switch to Daylight Saving Time (DST), as well as the Monday after employees lost an hour of sleep.

According to recent reports, on the Monday prior to DST, workers clicked on a phishing email link about 15.5 percent. of the time. Then, the Monday immediately following DST saw that rate rise to about 17.7 percent. That may not seem like much, but the difference comes out to about a 13 percent increase in phishing victims after losing approximately just one hour of sleep. According to Schechtman, there are multiple ways to contextualize these results.

Sources indicate that “First, they give us a peek into the effects of very minor sleep loss… [from] Daylight Saving Time, which is similar in scope to the kind of sleep loss that many of us experience daily,” he remarked. “Although we focused on cybersecurity, many of our day-to-day decisions are likely compromised in similar ways.”.

Schechtman hopes both employers and cybersecurity companies take regularly sleep-depriving events like DST, holidays, and even primetime sporting events into consideration when advising the public on phishing awareness. In the meantime, he stressed that even those who regularly suffer from sleep challenges continue to prioritize their rest as much as possible.

“Better sleep likely leads to better decisions,” he added.

Breaking: The 9 Most Beautiful States in the US

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, the most beautiful states in the US prove just how shockingly diverse the country is: volcanic beaches, glacier-capped peaks, canyon-carved deserts, and misty rainforests define their landscapes.
  • Hawaii is far from a monolithic state, with scenery changing from island to island.
  • Recent findings suggest that near Diamond Head, Doris Duke’s oceanfront estate, Shangri La, pairs 1930s modernism with architectural elements she brought from Morocco, Iran, Syria, and beyond.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, the most beautiful states in the US prove just how shockingly diverse the country is: volcanic beaches, glacier-capped peaks, canyon-carved deserts, and misty rainforests define their landscapes. What people have built in those places is just as varied, from a royal palace in downtown Honolulu to Mary Colter’s stone watchtower on the rim of the Grand Canyon to the cedar-shingled studios of a modernist craft school on the coast of Maine. These nine states stand out on both counts, for the scenery that defines them and the architecture that holds its own against it. Keep in mind that no ranking can settle which state is most beautiful—they’re all worthy of a visit.

Hawaii is far from a monolithic state, with scenery changing from island to island. In Honolulu on Oahu, ʻIolani Palace, completed in 1882 for King Kalākaua, is the only royal palace on US soil—and it had electricity before the White House did.

Recent findings suggest that near Diamond Head, Doris Duke’s oceanfront estate, Shangri La, pairs 1930s modernism with architectural elements she brought from Morocco, Iran, Syria, and beyond. It’s now a museum of Islamic art, with tours departing from the Honolulu Museum of Art.

As for the natural landscape, Kauai, known as the Garden Isle, is home to the Nā Pali Coast, where green ridges drop sharply toward the Pacific. On Maui, Haleakalā’s broad volcanic summit often rises above a blanket of clouds. And on the Significant Island, Hawaii Volcanoes National Park actively showcases the raw power of volcanoes—if you’re lucky, you might even catch an eruption.

Sources indicate that wyoming’s most famous photo moment might be the Teton Range rising abruptly above the sagebrush flats of Jackson Hole, ideally with one of Mormon Row’s weathered homestead barns in the foreground. Nearby, the tiny log Chapel of the Transfiguration, built in 1925, was sited so that the picture window behind its altar frames the peaks where stained glass would normally go.

In Yellowstone National Park, it’s all about color: Grand Prismatic Spring’s vivid rings stand out among the forested landscape, while the Grand Canyon of the Yellowstone exposes ochres and pinks in its steep walls. And steps from its namesake geyser, the Old Faithful Inn—designed by a 29-year-old Robert Reamer and opened in 1904—wraps a soaring lodgepole-pine lobby around a massive stone fireplace. It’s considered the largest log structure in the world.

Florida’s beaches are perhaps the state’s most scenic draw, but the architecture is just as distinctive. In 1979, Miami Beach’s Art Deco District, roughly a square mile of South Beach, became the nation’s first urban 20th-century historic district on the National Register, with more than 800 buildings listed. Across Biscayne Bay, industrialist James Deering’s Vizcaya, a villa completed in 1916, faces the water with formal gardens by Diego Suarez. Addison Mizner gave Palm Beach its Mediterranean Revival look; his Via Mizner, a winding pedestrian lane off Worth Avenue built in 1923, survives today.

Recent findings suggest that st. Augustine, founded by the Spanish in 1565, pairs the coquina-stone Castillo de San Marcos with Henry Flagler’s Hotel Ponce de Leon, a Spanish Renaissance–style palace from 1888 that’s now Flagler College. Architecture buffs should detour to Lakeland, where Frank Lloyd Wright’s campus for Florida Southern College is the largest single-site collection of his architecture in the world. And on the Gulf Coast, Sarasota’s midcentury modernists adapted the International Style to the subtropics, most famously in Paul Rudolph’s 1953 Umbrella House.

Sources indicate that on Maine’s coast, Acadia National Park packs a surprising amount of scenery into a small area: granite headlands, spruce forest, offshore islands, and views of the Atlantic. Look closely, and you'll notice the park’s impressive stonework, too. John D. Rockefeller Jr. financed its network of carriage roads, built between 1913 and 1940, along with 16 of the 17 stone-faced bridges that carry them over streams and gorges—no two are alike.

Don’t forget the coastal villages, from ever-popular Bar Harbor and its shingle-style and Queen Anne houses to Stonington, a working fishing town on Deer Isle. Elsewhere on Deer Isle, Edward Larrabee Barnes’s 1961 campus for the Haystack Mountain School of Crafts, an underrated masterpiece of American modernism, steps down a granite slope toward Jericho Bay, its cedar-shingled cabins and studios linked by boardwalks.

It has been revealed that california has a little of everything, from the architectural hubs of Los Angeles and San Francisco to breathtaking natural settings. In Yosemite, El Capitan and Half Dome are jaw-dropping from the valley floor, but even more so from the top for those daring enough to make the climb. Back down in the valley, the Ahwahnee hotel, which opened in 1927, appears to be built of granite and redwood—but the “wood” is actually fireproof concrete, poured into molds and stained to look like timber. In the desert, Palm Springs is a showcase of midcentury modernism, with Richard Neutra’s 1946 Kaufmann House as its best-known example.

Recent findings suggest that but the California coast is undeniably the state’s most famous landscape, and the 656 miles of Highway 1 deliver architecture along with the views. Above San Simeon, Hearst Castle, which Julia Morgan designed for William Randolph Hearst over nearly three decades, crowns a hilltop overlooking the Pacific. Continue north past the bluffs of Significant Sur and storybook Carmel-by-the-Sea to the Sonoma Coast, where the redwood-clad buildings of the Sea Ranch, a planned community begun in the mid-1960s, are tucked into hedgerows to leave the meadows and bluffs open.

Newly introduced York State’s famous architecture isn’t limited to the Manhattan skyline—though the city certainly pulls its weight on the architecture front. In the Adirondacks, wooded mountains surround lakes such as Lake Placid and the three Saranac Lakes. The “great camps” that wealthy families began building along their shores in the Gilded Age turned the log cabin into high style. You can still stay in one: The Point, on Upper Saranac Lake, was built in the early 1930s as Camp Wonundra for William Avery Rockefeller II and is now an 11-room Relais & Châteaux hotel, the first in North America.

In a recent development, in the Hudson Valley, painter Frederic Church’s hilltop villa, Olana, features a design style he called “Persian, adapted to the Occident.” The Finger Lakes offer a gentler landscape of long, narrow lakes bordered by vineyards and small towns, plus the gorge at Watkins Glen State Park, where a stone path meanders past tumbling cascades and swirling pools. And in Buffalo, you’ll find Frank Lloyd Wright’s Darwin D. Martin House, one of his finest Prairie-style designs.

It has been revealed that the Grand Canyon is a tough act to follow, but on its South Rim, architect Mary Colter spent decades designing buildings meant to hold their own beside it. Her Hopi House, which opened in 1905, is a multistory stone building shaped like a Hopi pueblo; her Desert View Watchtower, completed in 1932, is a 70-foot stone tower modeled on Ancestral Puebloan structures, with a Snake Legend mural inside by Hopi artist Fred Kabotie.

Sedona’s red-rock buttes are spectacular on their own, but the Chapel of the Holy Cross, a modernist concrete chapel built directly into a pair of sandstone buttes and completed in 1956, gives them a focal point. North of Phoenix, Paolo Soleri’s Arcosanti, an experimental desert town of concrete domes and arches begun in 1970, is still a work in progress. And in Scottsdale, in the foothills of the McDowell Mountains, Frank Lloyd Wright’s Taliesin West—his winter home and studio from 1937 until his death in 1959—is now a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

It has been revealed that texas’s landscapes range from the Chihuahuan Desert to the Gulf Coast to the bayous of Caddo Lake. In Significant Bend National Park, the Chisos Mountains rise above dry plains, and the Rio Grande cuts through the narrow walls of Santa Elena Canyon. In Marfa, minimalist artist Donald Judd turned a former army post into the Chinati Foundation, a museum built around permanent, large-scale installations, including his 100 mill-aluminum boxes lined up inside two converted artillery sheds.

According to recent reports, in Fort Worth, Louis Kahn’s Kimbell Art Museum, completed in 1972, draws architects from around the world to see natural light wash down its concrete cycloid vaults; Tadao Ando’s Modern Art Museum of Fort Worth sits just across the street. Central Texas has rolling hills, and in spring, bluebonnets and Indian paintbrush color the roadsides around Fredericksburg, a town with German heritage.

Sources indicate that mount Rainier is perhaps Washington’s most familiar landmark, its glaciers and snowfields visible above forests and summer wildflower meadows. The North Cascades offer even more peaks, with jagged ridges rising above turquoise Diablo Lake, while the trails in Olympic National Park lead through mossy rainforest and out to driftwood-strewn beaches.

Recent findings suggest that seattle holds its own against all that scenery. Downtown, the Central Library—designed by Rem Koolhaas’s OMA with local firm LMN and opened in 2004—wraps its stacked floors in a faceted net of glass and steel, while the Space Needle, built for the 1962 World’s Fair, remains the skyline’s signature. 📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sir Patrick Stewart, best-known for portraying Captain Jean-Luc Picard in “Star Trek” and Professor Charles Xavier in the “X-Men” film franchise, has died. He was 86.

The legendary actor and thespian passed away on October 28 after a “brief and poignant journey with Alzheimer’s Disease and Lewy Body Dementia,” according to his longtime spokesperson, Kelly Bush Novak, in a statement to The Hollywood Reporter.

He died peacefully at his home in Los Angeles, where he was receiving care from his wife, Sunny Ozell.

Industry observers note that “He has been held in the warm embrace of family and friends, surrounded by live music, prayer, tears, laughter and the kind of profound emotion that only he could inspire after a lifetime of devotion to us all,” Bush Novak wrote in the statement. “We will forever cherish the peaceful ease and reflection on his face, an enduring reminder of his invincible grace.”.

Stewart’s acting career spanned more than six decades across theater, television, and film.

A longtime member of the Royal Shakespeare Firm, he rose to international fame in 1987 with “Star Trek: The Next Generation” and later became known for his portrayal of Professor Charles Xavier in the 2000 film “X-Men” and its numerous sequels.

He was knighted by Queen Elizabeth II in 2010 for his contributions to drama.

Alzheimer’s disease and Lewy body dementia are two progressive neurological conditions that can affect memory, thinking, behavior, and a person’s ability to perform everyday activities.

According to the National Institute on Aging (NIA), both conditions can cause dementia, a term used to describe a decline in cognitive abilities severe enough to interfere with daily life.

Alzheimer’s disease is the most common cause of dementia. The condition is associated with abnormal buildups of proteins called amyloid and tau in the brain, which disrupt communication between nerve cells and contribute to their damage.

Sources indicate that the NIA states that memory problems are often among the earliest symptoms of Alzheimer’s. As the disease progresses, people may experience increasing difficulty with language, reasoning, decision making, and recognizing familiar people.

Lewy body dementia, meanwhile, is associated with abnormal deposits of a protein called alpha-synuclein in the brain. These deposits, known as Lewy bodies, affect brain chemicals involved in thinking, movement, mood, and sleep, according to the NIA.

People with Lewy body dementia may experience changes in attention and alertness, visual hallucinations, muscle stiffness, difficulty walking, and sleep disturbances.

According to the Alzheimer’s Association, the two conditions may co-occur, and their overlapping symptoms may make diagnosis more challenging.

Recent findings suggest that currently, neither condition has a cure, but treatments are available to help manage symptoms. Certain medications can also slow cognitive decline in some people with early Alzheimer’s disease.

Later Daters Still Love Sex

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (487 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Psychologytoday

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Posted November 16, 2026 | Reviewed by Ekua Hagan.
  • Among many destructive, ageist stereotypes prevalent in America, one of the most pervasive is that older adults aren’t interested in, capable of, or engaged in having sex.
  • While the stereotypes are alive and well regarding the nability of older adults to have sex, many, if not most, either do have, or are interested in having, sexual activity with a partner.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Posted November 16, 2026 | Reviewed by Ekua Hagan.

Among many destructive, ageist stereotypes prevalent in America, one of the most pervasive is that older adults aren’t interested in, capable of, or engaged in having sex. On the contrary, research highlights that about three-quarters of those aged 57-64, over half of those aged 65-74, and a quarter of those aged 75-85 had sexual contact with someone in the past year. And this doesn’t even count those who would have chosen to have sex but had no opportunity.

While the stereotypes are alive and well regarding the nability of older adults to have sex, many, if not most, either do have, or are interested in having, sexual activity with a partner. It’s true older adults may struggle with aspects of sex they didn’t confront when younger—men with the ability to maintain erections or ejaculate; women with lubrication or discomfort. But there are excellent treatments for these conditions, and humans are creative. Older adults engage in satisfying romantic relationships without sexual activity, satisfying sexual relationships without romance, and everything in between. And in terms of sex, older couples not only enjoy intercourse, but also non-penetrative sexual activities like hugging, cuddling, sleeping naked; manual, masturbatory, and oral play activities, and more.

Industry observers note that A recent study by Harris and Melanson (2026) interviewed 100 single older adults aged 60-83 (50 women and 50 men) recruited from dating sites for gender, racial, and educational diversity. More older adults are single today than ever before (due to longer lives and the acceptance of divorce), and this group is understudied compared to older adults with partners. The Harris and Melanson study was limited by heterosexual participants, but we can extrapolate many of its findings to all relationships:.

Sources indicate that sex is a healthy part of life throughout adulthood, whether one is single, partnered, or in between. How it looks and when it happens may change, and some adults may do well without a partner, but the majority of older adults, like younger adults, find partnered sex an vital ingredient of healthy social lives, life satisfaction, and wellbeing.

Sources indicate that harris and Melanson surveyed an often-ignored group of older adults—those who are single. Because they found them through dating sites, we know participants in the sample were at least somewhat interested in pursuing romantic and/or sexual partnerships. It’s up to future researchers to explore whether single older adults not interested in dating are equally interested in sex (with another person), or simply feel content alone; as well as how these results may be different in LGBTQ+ and other marginalized populations.

Recent findings suggest that harris, L., & Melanson, C. (2026). “The Shop Is Not Closed”: Sex and Sexuality Among Older Adult Daters. The Journal of Sex Research, 1–13. https://doi.org/10.1080/00224499.2026.2614315.

#5417. Tech Report: Baby chimpanzees blow ‘raspberries’ because adults do it first

📅 09 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (739 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Popsci ↗ Open Full Page

Tech Report: Baby chimpanzees blow ‘raspberries’ because adults do it first

📅 09 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (739 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Popsci

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that the old adage “monkey see, monkey do,” appears to have a bit of truth to it.
  • Humans learn what words mean from the world around us, and different communities will use different sounds for the same thing.
  • It has been revealed that to probe how chimpanzees learn to use sounds, the study’s team focused on the raspberry.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that the old adage “monkey see, monkey do,” appears to have a bit of truth to it. Chimpanzees (Pan troglodytes) likely watch adults making different vocalization to learn how and when to use those sounds themselves, particularly when they purse their lips to blow “raspberries.” The findings detailed in a study published today in the journal Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (PNAS) show that the primates’ sounds are not instinctual and set in stone, as previously believed.

Humans learn what words mean from the world around us, and different communities will use different sounds for the same thing. For example, English speakers mimic dogs with “woof,” while French speakers say “ouaf.” When it comes to our primate relatives, biologists generally used to believe that they didn’t learn sounds from one another, and that instead biology dictated their sounds. However, that’s changing with some latest research into two groups of Chimpanzees in a couple of west African countries.

It has been revealed that to probe how chimpanzees learn to use sounds, the study’s team focused on the raspberry. Chimpanzees make this unvoiced sound that’s similar to how humans push their lips together to blow raspberries. The team looked at how 91 chimpanzees, from birth to 55 years old, used the raspberry call. They studied a group of wild chimpanzees from four communities in Taï National Park, Ivory Coast, and a group of young, orphaned, and peer-raised chimpanzees at Tacugama Chimpanzee Sanctuary in Sierra Leone.

In a recent development, the team found that the wild Ivory Coast chimpanzees almost exclusively used the raspberry while grooming others. However, the juveniles at the Tacugama Chimpanzee Sanctuary used it across a much wider range of social situations.

It has been revealed that if blowing a raspberry is only an instinctive call, the groups should be using it in similar ways no matter where they were raised. According to the team, these differences suggest that chimpanzees learn from adults how to make a call, as well as when and why to use it.

In a recent development, “In everyday communication, we use the words that we do only because our peers do too. It’s communal practice that fixes their meaning, rather than features of the words themselves,” Richard Moore, a study co-author and mind, language, and psychology philosopher at the University of Warwick, mentioned in a statement.

“The discovery that this is true not just for natural languages but also some chimpanzee calls means there’s more continuity between chimpanzees’ vocal learning and our own than we previously suspected.”.

Sources indicate that the team also say that when an adult chimpanzee was introduced to one of the groups living in the Tacugama sanctuary, the young chimps gradually began to use the raspberry more consistently and began to resemble the adult’s noises. This suggests that adults serve as role models, helping a community settle in on shared communication patterns.

The researchers say this is the first time that this kind of learned and agreed-upon sound use has been shown in chimpanzee calls. The link between the raspberry sound and its use appears to be shared from one chimpanzee to another, and is not built in at birth. While chimpanzees struggle to learn entirely latest call sounds, the study suggests that they can learn the meaning behind sounds that they already know how to make but didn’t use in the same way as other chimps.

“Even aspects of chimpanzee vocal communication that seemed fixed and unlearned may be shaped by learning, suggesting that there is still much to discover about their vocal repertoire,”.

added Antoine Valet, a study co-author and cognitive scientist at the Institute of Cognitive Sciences (CNRS) in France.

Additionally, the team has some theories on why different chimpanzee populations use the raspberry in similar ways if it is a learned sound.

It has been revealed that “One possibility is that, whilst grooming, as chimpanzees use their lips to extract parasites from another’s fur, it may be easier to generate a vocalisation that uses similar lip movements, a call that is known to prolong grooming bouts,” explained study co-author and CNRS behavioral ecologist Catherine Crockford. “Communities may have found this useful independently, but that wouldn’t change the fact that the call is a convention. We need more research to test it.”.

The latest Mercedes-Benz EQS 450+ covered 539 miles without stopping to charge, making range anxiety look like a thing of the past.

Mercedes-Benz overhauled the EQS electric sedan, including a bigger battery and an 800V electrical architecture.

The 2027 Mercedes-Benz EQS 450+ uses a 122 kWh battery that provides an EPA-estimated range of up to 467 miles.

According to recent reports, while that’s already impressive, the electric sedan will likely go even farther in everyday driving conditions. During Edmunds recent EV Range Test, the 2027 Mercedes EQS 450+ drove a whopping 539 miles without stopping to charge.

The EQS beat its own EPA estimate by 72 miles and is now the longest-range electric sedan Edmunds has ever tested, beating the Lucid Air, the first EV to break the 500-mile mark. The only EV that has it beat is the Cadillac Escalade IQ, which managed 558 miles from its massive 205 kWh battery.

During the test, the 2027 Mercedes EQS 450+ was also more efficient than its official numbers suggest.

It has been revealed that the upcoming EQS used 29.6 kWh per 100 miles, beating its EPA estimate of 28 kWh per 100 miles. In comparison, the 2025 Mercedes EQS 450+ covered 464 miles and used 34 kWh per 100 miles during the same test, so the improvements are considerable.

Edmunds observed a peak charging rate of 350 kW, in line with Mercedes’ estimates, while it sustained an average of 222 kW throughout the session.

Both beat the older EQS, which reached a peak charge rate of 208 kW and sustained an average of 175 kW.

The new Mercedes EQS 450+ added 825 miles of range in an hour, and 100 miles in just over 7 minutes, nearly twice the speed of the 2025MY.

The Edmunds EV Range Test is designed to provide a more accurate estimate of an EV’s range in everyday driving conditions. It includes 60% city and 40% highway driving with an average speed of 40 mph. The vehicle stays within 5 mph of the posted speed limit, and the climate control is set to auto at 72 degrees.

How much is too much? 539 miles on a single charge is impressive, but do you need it? In a recent “nationally representative” survey, BMW found that Americans want more EV range than they actually need.

Sources indicate that the study demonstrated that 73% consider 25, 50, or 75 miles enough to cover their daily driving. However, 42% said they would require at least 300 miles of range before they would consider an EV.

If you have access to a home charger, nothing beats waking up with a full charge every day. Meanwhile, public charging continues to improve, giving EV drivers more reliable options on longer trips.

Faster charging also helps. Another 53% mentioned they would be more likely to consider an EV if it could add about 150 miles of range in around 10 minutes.

According to recent reports, in the same Edmunds EV Range Test last week, the newly introduced 2027 BMW iX3 50 xDrive drove 436 miles on a single charge, exceeding its EPA estimate of 392 miles by 44 miles. It also used 28.3 kWh per 100 miles during the test, beating its official EPA estimate of 32 kWh per 100 miles.

#5415. Human sacrifices were rare in ancient Peru, except when weather got violent

Human sacrifices were rare in ancient Peru, except when weather got violent

📅 09 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (601 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Popsci

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that today’s cataclysmic climate change-fueled disasters are scary enough even when we understand the root causes.
  • In a recent development, that said, researchers are now confident these periods of intense violence weren’t the norm—nor were they necessarily linked to climate issues.
  • “The main thing that jumped out at us was just how few cases of interpersonal violence we observed outside ritualized contexts,” noted Latest York University archaeologist and study co-author Thomas Snyder.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that today’s cataclysmic climate change-fueled disasters are scary enough even when we understand the root causes. Prehistoric cultures unfortunately didn’t have this luxury, and often responded dramatically to such changes. In northern Peru, archaeological evidence indicates local societies sometimes even turned to mass human sacrifices in an attempt to stop destructive flooding from events like El Niño.

In a recent development, that said, researchers are now confident these periods of intense violence weren’t the norm—nor were they necessarily linked to climate issues. According to their study recently published in Frontiers in Environmental Archaeology, such brutal moments were actually pretty rare occurrences in Peru’s Lambayeque Valley.

“The main thing that jumped out at us was just how few cases of interpersonal violence we observed outside ritualized contexts,” noted Latest York University archaeologist and study co-author Thomas Snyder.

In a recent development, the Lambayeque Valley is located inside northern Peru’s coastal desert, but the region has hosted residents for  6,000 years. Although the valley generally receives little rainfall, its rivers and proximity to the sea allowed communities to flourish there for generations, including societies like the Moche from roughly 100–750 CE, and the Sicán from about 750–1375 CE.

“Archaeological evidence reveals that in so many ways they were mirrors of us—in how they lived their daily lives, interacted with their world, ran their economies, and confronted (and sometimes contributed to) environmental crises,” explained George Mason University archaeologist and study co-author Haagen Klaus.

Industry observers note that previous excavations have indicated that mass human sacrifices possibly preceded the collapse of the Moche and Sicán’s political systems. Researchers have since hypothesized that these acts likely coincided with periods of mass flooding,probably due to El Niño weather oscillations. Just like today, these weather events destroyed food stocks and disrupted agricultural production. Since large human sacrificial rituals may have been attempts by the ruling class to restore balance to nature, the team to wonder if violence was simply a more common facet of everyday life for the Moche and Sicán.

“If these big ritual sacrifices were indicative of some underlying crisis, we hypothesized that these events might have been extending into people’s everyday experience of the world,” noted Snyder.

Klaus, Snyder, and their collaborators turned to the Lambayeque Valley Biohistory Project’s skeletal archive for answers. The collection spans about 3,000 years of history across 30 different archaeological sites. The team established relatively precise death estimates for over 1,600 individuals, while also examining them for evidence of intentional cranial trauma associated with human sacrifice. Contrary to their theory, only 25 remains (1.6 percent of the sample pool) showed signs of violence, while just 77 displayed indicators of accidental trauma. Of those, none were directly linked to known periods of past ecological crises.

“In Lambayeque, there’s 6,000 years of creative adaptations to El Niño and longer-term changes in climate, and widespread violence wasn’t one of them,” concluded Klaus.

Sources indicate that the study’s authors noted that because they were notable to radiocarbon date all of the remains, their findings remain broader estimates of wide time periods. At the same time, they stressed the evidence underscores humanity’s history of facing intense climate challenges not with violence, but adaptation.

According to recent reports, “This really highlights that widespread violence isn’t a predetermined response to climate change,” said Snyder. “As a society, we both get to and have to choose how we respond to our own climate crisis.”.

“Violence and social unraveling are not destined outcomes, ever,” added Klaus.

Driven: Porsche 911 Challenge Is a More Accessible Race Car

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1143 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Roadandtrack

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that next year will mark the 40th running of the Porsche Mobil 1 Supercup, the one-make race series so ubiquitous you hardly need either Porsche or 911 qualifiers for somebody to know what you mean by “Cup car.” Like other sports cars with long histories, the further you go back in time, the more similar the racing 911 is to the roadgoing version.
  • Sources indicate that early 964 Cup cars are, like Ferrari’s 355 Challenge, road legal with normal VIN codes.
  • It has been revealed that I tried the 992 Cup Car.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that next year will mark the 40th running of the Porsche Mobil 1 Supercup, the one-make race series so ubiquitous you hardly need either Porsche or 911 qualifiers for somebody to know what you mean by “Cup car.” Like other sports cars with long histories, the further you go back in time, the more similar the racing 911 is to the roadgoing version. Likewise, the further forward you move, the more they diverge.

Sources indicate that early 964 Cup cars are, like Ferrari’s 355 Challenge, road legal with normal VIN codes. They were stripped, caged versions of standard Carreras. I’m leaving out a lot of hardworking engineers’ tweaks here, but the point is that there was a time that driving a Cup car felt mostly like a normal car with more noise, fewer comforts, and better safety equipment. The 1999 996-generation Cup still used a coded key and had a normal clutch and an H-pattern 6-speed—it was just a very sticky GT3. But the 997 generation of 2005 was the fork in the road, introducing a sequential gearbox. The 2013 991-gen brought in a motorsport engine-management system and electronics. And the 992 generation that races today nominally resembles a 911 but operates nothing like one and requires a team to run it.

It has been revealed that I tried the 992 Cup Car. It is incredibly intimidating. I do not have what it takes to be successful in a car like that, and I would not want to have to round up a posse to go for a drive, even if the performance is staggering. Instead what I really want, as do many other amateur and wannabe racers, is a race car that closely resembles their road car. Hence the popularity of the GT3 RS. If the car never leaves the track property, why get a GT3 RS when you could get an Oreca LMP for $100k less? Because it’s not really about being street legal; it’s about being approachable and turnkey.

The car for regular weekend warriors used to be the GT4/RS Clubsport, but sadly, the 718-generation Cayman is now dead and buried. Earlier this year, rumors swirled that Porsche was prepping a 911 GT4 to take the Cayman’s place, and the story ran alongside photos of a racy-looking camouflaged 992 GT3. It turns out that Porsche is going GT4 racing with the 911, but that will be a modified Cup car, not the one from those pictures. Instead, the images were of the car you see here, the latest 911 Challenge. Essentially, it’s the old GT3 Cup car concept for today’s country-club weekend warriors: an upfitted, stripped, and caged GT3 road car.

A roll cage can only make a car so approachable, but once I’d stopped and crawled into the comfy seat, things got familiar quickly, as I was looking at the complete 992-generation dashboard, gauge cluster, and center console. The steering wheel is straight out of the GT3 RS (though without an airbag installed). After strapping in with the multipoint harnesses,I pressed the original start button on the left, and the 4.0-liter flat-six fired just like a standard GT3. The Challenge retains the factory heating and ventilation; the road car’s touchscreen display is gone, replaced by a blank panel with emergency cutoff and fire switches.

Sources indicate that mechanically, it’s barely changed from the GT3. The engine makes six more horsepower, now 508 hp total, thanks to a race-specific exhaust setup. But it still uses the standard, seven-speed PDK dual-clutch transmission, so you can just put it in drive if you prefer, or shift using the paddles.

Industry observers note that my drive in the Challenge was brief. Just four laps around the 2.5-mile Circuit Ricardo Tormo, following on from my four-car Manthey test. For context, with factory race driver Timo Bernhard driving this circuit, the Challenge almost perfectly splits the range: 4.6 seconds per lap slower than a Cup, and 5.2 seconds quicker than a GT3 Weissach. Notably, it’s also 1.6 seconds quicker per lap than the GT3 RS Manthey. Where it gets interesting is in the details.

A GT3 RS Manthey is on road-legal tires but with enormous downforce. The Challenge is on slicks but with the same aero package as a standard GT3.

So if you’re willing to throw away street legality, for $275,000 (less than the cost of many standard GT3s) you can go far quicker on a track than you could with the fastest road-legal 911 you can buy, the Manthey GT3 RS, which would knock on the door of half a million dollars.

Everything about the Challenge is easy. As long as you’re reasonably comfortable on a slick tire, the rest of the car comes directly to you. The Challenge is far more reliant on mechanical grip than downforce, so you can start learning the car by going much quicker through hairpins than you ever have before, rather than having to learn it by going full send over a blind crest in sixth gear, with potentially scary consequences.

According to recent reports, likewise, because there isn’t 2200 pounds of downforce, the Challenge isn’t sprung too stiffly, so you don’t take abuse on bumpy curbing. The knobs for traction control and PTV work essentially the same as the GT3 RS, just with fresh programming specific to the Challenge.

Sources indicate that I’m not going to pretend, in five laps, to have a thorough understanding of the dynamics of the 911 Challenge, or to say that I took it to its limit. I had just enough time to get comfortable, which is more than I can say about other race cars.

What I did have was an incredible time on the track. The Challenge is the kind of car that inspired me to want to push it harder, but the “race car” bits of it disappeared into the background, so I could focus on things happening outside rather than things inside. It was instantly comfortable and familiar, and a place I could spend all day. Three-hour double stint in an enduro? That would be no problem. Also, possible thanks to the 29-gallon fuel cell.

There will be a one-make series for the 911 Challenge, and initially Porsche wants to sell them to folks who intend to enter, but that’s not really the point—this is the 911 race car that most 911 owners actually want. It is a fun, flexible, approachable, and fizzy experience that elevates what they already love about the 911 and can race if they want to, but that won’t require a whole team if they just want to rip off a few laps after work. And for less money than the road car, not more.

It’s the race car for people who want their race car to feel like a 911, not like a corporation.
