💡 Key Takeaways
  • Only 8,817 of the cars Tesla delivered from Giga Shanghai in October went to Chinese buyers.
  • Back in July 2022, the Shanghai factory was partly shut down for line upgrades.
  • It has been revealed that the China Passenger Car Association (CPCA) reported that Tesla China wholesaled 67,829 vehicles in October, up 10.3% year-over-year.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Only 8,817 of the cars Tesla delivered from Giga Shanghai in October went to Chinese buyers. That’s down 66% from a year ago and Tesla’s worst month in China since July 2022, according to CPCA data.

Back in July 2022, the Shanghai factory was partly shut down for line upgrades. This time it ran normally and shipped 87% of what it built out of the country.

It has been revealed that the China Passenger Car Association (CPCA) reported that Tesla China wholesaled 67,829 vehicles in October, up 10.3% year-over-year. That’s the number most headlines ran with.

But 59,012 of those were exports. Strip them out and you’re left with 8,817 cars for the domestic market, the one Giga Shanghai was originally built to serve.

According to recent reports, nearly all of them were Model Ys (7,807), according to CnEVPost, leaving just 1,010 Model 3s. And compared to September, when Tesla sold 64,837 cars in China, domestic sales fell 86%.

Here’s how October has looked over the last three years:.

Tesla favors export orders early in each quarter and pushes domestic deliveries toward the end of it, and September’s promotions and quarter-end rush pulled some demand forward.

That’s real. Tesla’s China sales have followed this sawtooth pattern for years. Last October was also weak, and Tesla then delivered 73,145 cars in China in November and 93,843 in December.

According to recent reports, but it doesn’t explain the size of this drop. Here’s every first month of a quarter in 2026:.

October is less than half of the previous low this year. And the October trough keeps getting deeper: 40,485 in 2024, 26,006 in 2025, 8,817 now.

In a recent development, china’s EV market is having a rough year. NEV retail sales fell 10% year-over-year in October to 1.148 million units, according to CPCA’s preliminary data, as Beijing phases out trade-in subsidies and the NEV purchase tax exemption was cut in half on January 1. The overall passenger car market was down 25%.

Tesla was down 66%. That works out to about 0.8% of China’s NEV retail market last month.

In a recent development, meanwhile, Xiaomi, which only started delivering cars in 2024, delivered more than 50,000 vehicles in October. Leapmotor delivered 106,127, up 51%. BYD delivered 490,168, though that includes its exports.

Through October, Tesla has sold 389,905 cars in China. That’s down 15% from 458,710 over the same period last year and its lowest January-to-October total in at least four years:.

The decline is speeding up. Tesla was down 11.9% in China through September, and one bad October pushed that to 15%. This year is now 22% below the 2024 peak, or about 110,000 fewer cars.

Exports from Giga Shanghai went the other way, up 101% to 420,984.

So this year, Shanghai has now shipped more cars abroad than it sold at home. Last year, domestic sales beat exports by more than two to one.

As we reported last month, Beijing is cutting the VAT export rebate on EVs from 13% to 9% on April 1, 2027, with the rate set by the customs declaration date. We mentioned to expect automakers to cram exports in ahead of the deadline. October’s 59,012 exports, up 66% year-over-year, fit that.

Industry observers note that we’ve been tracking this gap all year, from Tesla’s Q1 China retail crash to the first-half numbers. Every time, the wholesale headline looks fine and the domestic number underneath gets worse. October is the most extreme version yet: Tesla China “grew” 10% while Chinese buyers bought 66% fewer Teslas.

We don’t buy that this is just the quarterly cycle. The cycle explains why October is weaker than September. It doesn’t explain why this October is a third of last October, or less than half of any other month this year.

In a recent development, I've been saying this for the last two years. Tesla's problem isn't that Elon temporarily alienated customers in Europe or other countries. Yes that killed sales for a bit, but in the end people are practical and will buy the best car for the money. And we saw that is exactly what happened with European Tesla sales coming back when gas prices rose and Tesla as a package (quality + price) was still very competitive.

The real problem that Tesla has is that they're falling behind in China not because anyone cares about Elon's politics, but because the cars are just less and less competitive. And while the Chinese competition doubles down on vehicle development and rolls out a new car every week, Tesla has lost all interest in it. There is absolutely nothing on the horizon for them in terms of new vehicles that consumers can buy. Looks like the 3 and Y are all they will have and no updates are coming.

I know, FSD or bust, but that's also assuming Chinese brands don't crack that nut at the same time.

Recent findings suggest that two things can be true at once. The export numbers show Tesla front-loading shipments ahead of the rebate cut. And Chinese demand for a Model 3 and Model Y lineup that hasn’t fundamentally changed in years keeps fading while Xiaomi, Leapmotor and BYD launch upcoming models every few months.

And if Tesla is choosing to send cars abroad instead of selling them in China, that’s not exactly a vote of confidence in its Chinese business either.

The real test is November and December. Last year, Tesla bounced back to 73,000 and 94,000 domestic sales. If it gets close to that again, October was mostly timing. If it doesn’t, Tesla has a serious problem in the world’s largest EV market, and the export valve that’s been hiding it gets more expensive in April.

#5379. Breaking: Can AI Companions Really Solve Loneliness?

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1105 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Psychologytoday ↗ Open Full Page

Breaking: Can AI Companions Really Solve Loneliness?

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1105 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Psychologytoday

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Posted November 16, 2026 | Reviewed by Ekua Hagan.
  • Recent findings suggest that engagement with artificial intelligence seems to be everywhere today, from education to medicine to business to making day-to-day life easier.
  • Sources indicate that there may be incredible potential for AI to advance human happiness, health, and financial security.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Posted November 16, 2026 | Reviewed by Ekua Hagan.

Recent findings suggest that engagement with artificial intelligence seems to be everywhere today, from education to medicine to business to making day-to-day life easier. Undoubtedly, some uses will prove beneficial, and others harmful. Evaluating the effect of different forms of AI engagement on human flourishing will thus be critical, and we believe our flourishing measure provides a helpful framework by which to do so. The effects of AI on flourishing may also differ across domains of flourishing.

Sources indicate that there may be incredible potential for AI to advance human happiness, health, and financial security. It is not guaranteed to do so, and indeed, as per Pope Leo XIV’s recent encyclical Magnifica Humanitas (Magnificent Humanity), much of what AI does or does not achieve will depend upon whether the human person and human dignity are made central in the use and diffusion of AI. However, if employed well and equitably, the potential for AI to advance these aspects of human well-being may be substantial.

The effects, however, of AI technologies on more humanistic aspects of well-being, such as meaning, character, or relationships, seem more ambiguous. Rich, developed countries already seem to be struggling with these more humanistic aspects of well-being, possibly in part due to technology. Will AI help or hinder our sense of meaning, our character, our relationships? As always, so much depends on how we use it.

Sources indicate that AI technologies with various relational elements have effectively been used for purposes ranging from helping autistic children develop social skills to building the capacity of university students for civil discourse. While such uses arguably always ought to point back to real relationships, these systems may indeed have the potential to truly enhance human relationships.

However, there is another class of chatbots that aims not at enhancing human relationships, but at replacing them. These are chatbots whose principal aim and purpose is friendship and romance. In a recent article, we have argued that such friendship and romance chatbots have no place in a flourishing life. This may seem like an extreme position. After all, what harm is there in having loneliness somewhat relieved if one’s friends or family are proving disappointing?

Recent findings suggest that the problem is that the temporary alleviation of loneliness is not a solution to loneliness. Loneliness, as painful as it can be, is experienced precisely to try to direct our attention, and our longings, towards deeper human connection. That can take a lot of work and time, and may not be fully within our grasp. But that thirst for human connection has a fundamental role in our life, in guiding us towards others.

When AI chatbots have, as their goal, not helping us with human relationships, but replacing them, they will do damage—damage to ourselves, damage to those we might have interacted with, and damage to the social fabric of society. If they satisfy our loneliness, they do so without another person. A chatbot that always seems to understand, that never has needs of its own, that treats neglect with a delight to see us, ultimately makes us weaker in our capacity for real human relationships. We come to have unrealistic expectations of what to hope for in real human relationships. We lose the capacity to grow through the very difficulties and frictions that real human relationships entail. We come to focus on ourselves rather than on providing for the needs of others. Indeed, with AI friendship and romance, there is no one on the other side to whose life we have contributed.

Industry observers note that while AI may have some capacity to enhance our relationships (pointing us towards helpful books or resources for particular problems we are wrestling with) and while certain AI chatbot applications may benefit from relational elements (like the training programs above), this is very different from AI chatbots aimed at replacing real relationships. The effects of these are universally and comprehensively detrimental. They harm us, and they harm those around us. Even if we do not feel the negative effects now, or if they seem small, the increasing incapacity for social relationships will over time gradually erode human connection, human community, and the fabric of society. Human relationships are critical for our health and well-being.

In a remarkable turn of events, China, which has been very pro-AI, in July put into place comprehensive legislation restricting the development and marketing of AI tools “that provide emotional care, companionship, support, and other emotional services,” and including a strict ban on tools “excessively pandering to consumers, inducing emotional reliance or addiction, [or] harming users' relationships with real people.” What does China know that we don’t? They seem to have almost presciently anticipated the likely effects of AI romance and relationships on human society, human relationships, human reproduction, and human community.

According to recent reports, there have also recently been some helpful legislative efforts here in the United States, especially for minors. However, we are naïve to think children are the only ones at risk.

It has been revealed that while we do think a ban on AI “relationship chatbots” for friendship and romance may be reasonable here (after all, we ban heroin in the United States), some might view such measures as too extreme. Even if so, we nevertheless believe every effort should be made in practice to purge AI friendship and romance from our lives as individuals and as communities. A technology designed to replace human connection is not a neutral technology.

Love—including love of neighbor and even love of enemy—is crucial for the flourishing of our society. In the words of Pope Leo (and others before him), if we are to seek a flourishing society (and to do so in the age of AI), we need to build “a civilization of love.” We need to love and care for one another. We need to be with one another. We need to have the capacity to work through the difficulties and frictions that real relationships entail, and to grow through those struggles. Therein lies our flourishing, for ourselves, for others, and for society. Real human love requires real human people.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The “world’s leading ice cream truck manufacturer” has released its first fully electric ice cream truck, which is already in operaiton, and it notes it’s open for orders for more.

Whitby Morrison bills itself as “the world’s leading ice cream truck manufacturer,” supplying converted vans as ice cream trucks to drivers worldwide.

And now it has taken a big step into the modern age delivering its first fully electric ice cream truck to Hocking’s dairy in North Devon, England.

The truck has been operating since July, through the course of one “ice cream season.” It reportedly covered more than 100 miles a day and has done days serving up to 12 hours at a time.

Industry observers note that it’s built on a standard Mercedes eSprinter, so it’s not retrofitted from the diesel vans that make up most of Whitby Morrison’s other offerings. The eSprinter comes in a “chassis cab” configuration which comes with just the chassis and cab, and lets upfitters build whatever they want onto the back end of the vehicle.

In this case, it also got some pretty extensive (and a little over-the-top) art all around the vehicle, highlighting the van’s electric operation.

The ice cream truck maker, Whitby Morrison, notes this is the “world’s first fully certified electric ice cream truck.”.

Recent findings suggest that we’re not sure what sort of international certifications are required for an ice cream truck so we’ll take their word for it, but we have seen a Rivian EDV turned into a Ben & Jerry’s ice cream truck, complete with side window, and a concept electric ice cream truck as far back as 2019. So it’s certainly not the very first time this idea has been had, at least.

And it is a good idea. As with school buses, ice cream trucks are vehicles that children are likely to congregate around. Having a stinky old truck spewing emissions just a few feet away from those kids’ lungs is the sort of thing that can expose them to a life of health problems… and we might as well not stack that on top of the sugar addiction we’re teaching them to have (hey, at least they have to get outside to chase the truck down, so they’re getting some physical activity out of it, right?).

It also opens up more possibilities for operators to serve at events where having a diesel truck running might not be reasonable, like in enclosed spaces or where quiet might be appreciated (this came up when we went to Harbinger Motors’ factory opening, where local food trucks were in attendance, inside the large factory building, and made the air quality noticeably worse).

Whitby Morrison claims it’s taking orders both in the UK and overseas, with US orders just opening. To learn more, head on over to its website.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Yes, bears are big. Depending on the time of year and sex, the average black bear (Ursus americanus) weighs between 90 to 500 pounds. On average brown bears (Ursus arctos) can weigh between 600 to 900 pounds. However, one female black bear named Volverine is a true fat bear queen this year. The U.S. Forest Service team at Tongass National Forest in southeastern Alaska have awarded her with the 2026 Big & Beautiful Award for her heft.

The rangers say that this mother bear is a “true icon,” who will often pose on a rock for a long time, seemingly allowing the visitors to Anan Wildlife Observatory to take photos. She is regarded as one of the most beautiful bears at Anan, with a chest patch shaped like the letter V. Volverine is also on the bigger end of the black bear spectrum, with a potato-shaped body, and an especially round butt. Her fishing skills made her one of the largest bears of the 2026 season—and a dominant matriarch.

“Our rangers love to see a fat female bear because that could mean cubs next year!” the rangers write. “Bears have what’s called delayed implantation, meaning they mate in the spring, and IF they get fat enough, the embryos implant in the fall.”.

Wishing Volverine and all of the bears the best this winter season.

The rangers at Tongass National Forest are currently awarding the Anan Bear Awards to the 39 bears spotted at the Anan Wildlife Observatory in Alaska over the summer.

Tongass is the largest national forest in the United States, and covers most of southeastern Alaska, including the state’s capital city of Juneau. The area includes Mendenhall Glacier (a popular destination for Alaskan cruises), hiking trails, eagles soaring above, and plenty of bears. One of the hotspots is Anan Creek, home to one of the largest runs of pink salmon in Southeast Alaska. The run is a very popular dinner spot among black and brown bears.

According to Friends of Anan, 39 bears are known to feast on the salmon at Anan Creek. The population includes 31 black bears and eight brown bears. Like their chunky counterparts farther to the north in Katmai National Park, the bears return each summer to feast on salmon and teach their cubs how to fish in order to survive. And also like the fat bears of Katmai, every bear here has their own habits and quirks. Volverine would fit right in with Katmai’s chunky brown bears, despite the fact that black bears tend to be a bit smaller.

Recent findings suggest that the U.S. Forest Service tracks and documents every bear spotted at Anan, while explore.org’s cameras broadcast live streams of what they are up to 24/7.

Industry News: Losing Weight in Your 50s May Protect Your Heart Health Later in Life

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Losing weight in your 50s, even a modest amount, may help protect your heart health later in life, according to upcoming research.Adults who lost weight in their early 50s saw their blood pressure, “good” cholesterol and inflammation change at about the same rate as adults who stayed at a healthy weight, according to a study from researchers at University College London and the University of Glasgow.Adults who gained weight in their early 50s saw those same measures worsen faster by their early 60s, the researchers reported.
  • Industry observers note that charis Bridger-Staatz, PhD, a senior research fellow at UCL, led the study.
  • The findings can apply to Americans because British and U.S.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Losing weight in your 50s, even a modest amount, may help protect your heart health later in life, according to upcoming research.Adults who lost weight in their early 50s saw their blood pressure, “good” cholesterol and inflammation change at about the same rate as adults who stayed at a healthy weight, according to a study from researchers at University College London and the University of Glasgow.Adults who gained weight in their early 50s saw those same measures worsen faster by their early 60s, the researchers reported. The authors posted the study on a research-sharing website on September 4. Other scientists have not yet peer-reviewed the work.

Industry observers note that charis Bridger-Staatz, PhD, a senior research fellow at UCL, led the study. She told Healthline the main takeaway for adults over 50 was that “it’s not too late to try and do things that are going to improve your health.”Nearly half of U.S. adults ages 40 to 59 had obesity from 2021 to 2023, the highest rate of any adult age group, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC). Among all U.S. adults, around 31.7% were overweight, according to the CDC.

The findings can apply to Americans because British and U.S. adults share similar weight patterns, stated Solveig Cunningham, PhD, a professor of global health at Emory University’s Rollins School of Public Health. Cunningham, who was not involved in the research, told Healthline that Americans tend to gain weight across adulthood.

Industry observers note that “By the time you get into your 50s, close to the majority of Americans already have obesity. Many others have overweight,” she stated.The World Health Organization (WHO) calls obesity a chronic disease. Healthcare professionals diagnose overweight and obesity using a person’s weight and height, or body mass index (BMI).

Bridger-Staatz said the team set out to learn who lost weight and kept it off before GLP-1 weight loss medications became available, and whether that weight loss improved health over time.

According to recent reports, she noted researchers had long assumed that “once people had become overweight or developed obesity, people didn’t really lose weight and certainly not sustained it.”The team also asked, she said, “can we try and say something positive about health that isn’t just this kind of like doom and gloom?”The researchers used the British 1958 National Child Development Study, which has followed about 17,500 people born during one week in 1958. Of those, 6,309 took part in a health check in their early 60s, according to the report.The team compared each person’s highest weight between ages 23 and 42 with their weight between ages 50 and 55. Researchers sorted people by whether they gained or lost more than 5% of their body weight and kept the change. For a 200-pound person, 5% equals 10 pounds.To track heart health, the team compared blood tests and blood pressure readings at ages 44 and 62 with those of people who maintained a healthy weight.“We know everyone’s heart health is kind of going to get a little bit worse over that time because you are aging and that’s expected,” Bridger-Staatz said. The question, she said, was, “Does it slow the rate at which people’s heart health is getting worse?”.

Industry observers note that weight loss slowed the decline in heart health for people who were overweight and for people with obesity, according to the report.People who were overweight and lost weight had the strongest positive results. By age 62, their body fat-to-lean tissue ratio matched that of the healthy-weight group. The authors wrote that differences in body fat may partly explain why weight changes affected heart health.People with obesity who lost weight had less body fat at 62 than people in the other obesity groups, according to the report.Sudhakara Chennareddy, MD, prevention cardiologist in the Center for Cardiovascular Prevention, Metabolism and Lipids at Georgia Heart Institute, told Healthline those results are what he’d expect. He was not involved in the research.“Even losing 5% has beneficial effects on the cardiovascular side effects,” he stated. Long-term blood sugar was the exception. For people with obesity who lost weight, it rose more than in the healthy-weight group, though the authors reported that the result was not statistically significant.

Industry observers note that A 2025 study of more than 15,000 U.S. adults, published in Endocrinology, Diabetes & Metabolism, found that adults who had previously had obesity tended to have higher blood sugar than those who had never had it, even after their BMI dropped.

Recent findings suggest that “It’s not the patient’s fault… We need to treat this one like any other chronic disease, like we treat hypertension or we treat diabetes,” Chennareddy noted.Compared with the healthy-weight group, people who gained weight in their early 50s had faster increases in blood pressure, blood fats, and inflammation, and declines in “good” cholesterol. Obesity is a chronic metabolic disease that leads to inflammation in the body, which can raise the risk of heart attack and stroke and worsen cholesterol levels, Chennareddy said. “The more weight they gain, they develop prediabetes and diabetes and fatty liver disease as well,” he said.These changes were largest for people who developed obesity or already had obesity and gained more weight, the researchers reported. This group also saw faster increases in long-term blood sugar levels.About 37% of participants gained more than 5% of their body weight in their early 50s. Only about 6% lost weight and kept it off, according to the study.“To me, that’s sort of the stronger message,” Cunningham said of the findings. Her advice for adults in their 50s is to avoid gaining weight.

People with obesity who lost and then gained the weight back saw faster drops in “good” cholesterol and faster rises in inflammation and long-term blood sugar.

By age 62, they weighed slightly less, on average, than people whose obesity remained steady, according to the report’s data. They also carried more body fat and had more inflammation.Weight cycling can do more harm than steady weight, Chennareddy mentioned. He gave the example of someone who gains 20 pounds, loses 30 and then gains 20 again. “That is even more detrimental,” he said.When people lose weight, the body slows its resting metabolism, he said. When the weight comes back, “most of the weight they gain is fat, not muscle,” he said. Even someone who loses and regains 5% to 7% of their body weight may end up with slightly less muscle and more fat, he said.Some research has shown that weight fluctuation is associated with a higher risk of high blood pressure and cardiovascular disease-related death.

The study’s weight changes took place between about 2008 and 2013, according to the study’s timeline.

In a recent development, wegovy, a GLP-1 medication for weight management, launched in the United Kingdom in September 2023, according to the UK Department of Health and Social Care.Cunningham stated the weight-cycling findings raised questions for people who take GLP-1 medications. She said drugmakers’ own data show that “once you get off of those, your weight is going to go right back to where it was before, possibly even worse.”That could create the same up-and-down pattern, Cunningham said. She added that researchers don’t yet know “what happens in the really long term” for people who take these medications.

According to recent reports, the study revealed links between weight changes and heart health and cannot prove that weight changes caused the results, according to the authors. They wrote that the small number of people who lost weight made those results less precise.Bridger-Staatz also said the team did not look at why or how people lost weight.

Cunningham said adults lose muscle and bone mass with age, and that the loss is especially pronounced for women in their 50s and older. “Maintaining muscles and maintaining bones is so, so important,” she said.Staying active helps people keep muscle, even without weight loss, Cunningham said. “Even a little bit of activity…just keep moving,” she said.GLP-1 medications work best as part of a “comprehensive plan,” Chennareddy said. With his patients, he said he recommends continuous improvement rather than setting a goal to lose a specific amount of weight within a set period.Patients who treat weight loss as “a gradual process” do better long term, he said.“The most important thing is not to do fad diets,” Chennareddy said.For people losing weight, Chennareddy recommended:.

Anyone considering changes to their weight can talk with a healthcare professional about their weight history and goals.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that juiced Bikes is expanding its recently relaunched Scrambler lineup with a upcoming, more affordable model known as the Juiced Scrambler Core. The new bike keeps much of the moto-inspired styling and performance of the existing Scrambler Hardtail, but trims back several components to knock several hundred dollars off the price.

The new Scrambler Core starts at $1,399, compared to $1,699 for the existing Scrambler Hardtail.

Juiced is also offering a $1,599 long-range version of the Core, as well as a smaller “Midsize” frame that should make the bike much more accessible to shorter riders – and, perhaps more importantly, teenagers.

Teens are a major part of the moto-style e-bike market, and Juiced has designed its Scrambler e-bikes as a safer option for those younger riders. In addition to ensuring street-legal performance for most major markets, Juiced rolled out a feature known as Speed Lock, which is essentially a parental control option that lets a parent or guardian set a lower speed limit using a PIN code that prevents their teen from later modifying the speed limit.

Sources indicate that the launch comes as part of the rebirth of Juiced Bikes following the brand’s acquisition last year. The tech giant was founded in 2009 and was acquired in 2025 by the co-founders of Lectric Ebikes, who have since brought the brand back with a upcoming generation of its popular Scrambler platform.

The biggest changes appear to be in the powertrain, battery, brakes, and suspension.

The standard Scrambler Hardtail launched earlier this year set the standard for the flagship models by using a 750W nominal motor with 90 Nm of torque and reaching 28 mph (45 km/h). Its 52V 19.2Ah battery provides nearly 1 kWh of capacity and a claimed range of up to 60 miles (96 km).

It has been revealed that the Scrambler Core steps down to a 500W nominal rear hub motor rated for 1,176W peak and 80 Nm of torque. Top speed is also reduced slightly to 25 mph (40 km/h), while the throttle is limited to 20 mph (32 km/h). Importantly, though, Juiced has retained its 52V architecture, meaning this is still a fairly punchy setup rather than a dramatically detuned budget bike.

Battery capacity takes a hit as well. The standard Core gets a 52V 10Ah battery with 520 Wh of capacity, rated for up to 40 miles (64 km) of range. Spending another $200 gets the Core Long-Range with a 52V 15Ah, 780Wh battery and a claimed 60-mile (96 km) maximum range. As with nearly all e-bikes, expect real-world range to fall short of the idealized advertised numbers, which are generally only achievable under the lowest power pedal assist.

Juiced also traded the Talon P4 four-piston hydraulic brakes found on the more expensive Scrambler for Talon P2 two-piston brakes. The KKE inverted fork with 140mm of travel is gone too, replaced by a more conventional aluminum triple-crown fork with 100mm of travel.

Recent findings suggest that those are meaningful downgrades, but they’re also largely the kinds of changes I’d expect to see when trying to shave $300 off an already competitively priced moto-style e-bike. It’s a strategy we’ve seen play out before in the industry, helping lower costs for riders who want a flagship bike but don’t necessarily want to pay flagship prices.

Even so, notable features remain to help maintain the look and feel of the Juiced Scrambler line. The Core still gets 20 x 4-inch fat tires, hydraulic disc brakes, a frame-integrated TFT display, four pedal-assist levels, a headlight, taillight, brake light, and turn signals. It’s a single-speed setup and weighs 73 lb (33 kg), while being rated for a 300 lb (136 kg) payload.

Perhaps the more interesting addition is the Scrambler Core Midsize.

Sources indicate that while the regular Core is recommended for riders 5’2” and taller, the Midsize drops that figure to just 4’10”. Pricing remains the same: $1,399 with the 520Wh battery or $1,599 with the 780Wh long-range pack.

It has been revealed that and with an eye towards safety, the Core and Core Mini retain Juiced’s PIN-protected parental speed lock. Parents can set the motor-assisted top speed anywhere from 1-25 mph and lock the setting behind a four-digit PIN. That makes even more sense on the Midsize version, which seems tailor-made for younger riders who want the moto-style look but may not yet comfortably fit the larger Scrambler.

The Core is launching in several decidedly Juiced color names, including Black Nectar, Fruit Punch, Sour Grape, White Grape, Berry Freeze, and Blood Orange, though availability varies between frame sizes and battery configurations. Juiced indicates preorders are expected to begin shipping around the end of the month.

Recent findings suggest that at $1,399, the Scrambler Core feels like a logical extension of Juiced’s rebooted lineup. You lose some battery, motor power, braking hardware, suspension travel, and a few mph compared to the Hardtail, but the underlying recipe is largely intact. For riders who mostly want the Scrambler look and feel – or parents shopping for a smaller rider – saving $300 may be a pretty compelling trade. Especially when you consider that the original Juiced Scrambler already led the industry in value for moto-style e-bikes from reputable brands.

Toss in the strong backing from Lectric and the 3-year warranty, and it’s hard to consider much else among the competition.

Latest Update: What Is the Strongest Predictor of Divorce?

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (743 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Psychologytoday

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Posted November 16, 2026 | Reviewed by Michelle Quirk.
  • By definition, all married couples seek to avoid their marriage falling apart.
  • Getting divorced increases one’s risk of experiencing financial strain, drug and alcohol abuse, suicide, poorer health, and interrupted parenting if the couple has children.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Posted November 16, 2026 | Reviewed by Michelle Quirk.

How do you avoid getting divorced? By definition, all married couples seek to avoid their marriage falling apart. In wedding ceremonial vows, couples make commitments to each other, which typically include standing by one another’s side in sickness and health, and in times of prosperity and poverty. Marriage is meant to last forever, but it doesn’t always work out as intended. In the United States, 43-46 percent of marriages end in divorce, and that number rises for second or third marriages.1.

Divorce is painful and costly. Getting divorced increases one’s risk of experiencing financial strain, drug and alcohol abuse, suicide, poorer health, and interrupted parenting if the couple has children. Despite the high prevalence of divorce and the substantial consequences associated with it, research on why marriages end has largely developed in separate camps: one focused on how couples communicate, another on the personal vulnerabilities each spouse brings into the marriage, and a third on couples’ financial and socioeconomic circumstances. These perspectives had never been directly compared to see which best predicts divorce. Recently, a team of social scientists published an article digging deep into this question.2.

In a recent development, the researchers began by recruiting 368 heterosexual newlywed couples from the Los Angeles Project on Newlywed Development who had gotten married within the past 6 months. The study began in 2009-10 and concluded in 2021-22. Over these 12 years, the researchers tracked a variety of metrics from the couples and, of primary interest, which couples got divorced (or were separated). Six key predictor variables were collected, which include:.

The vulnerability variables included a score composed of adverse childhood experiences, history of physical/sexual abuse, problematic substance use (past 9 months), negative affect (past 30 days), and parents’ marital status. Communication style was assessed by video recording couples’ discussion of a topic or problem in their relationship, which was carefully coded by trained research assistants. Socioeconomic status included typical metrics of education, income, work stability, financial strain, and neighborhood median income. Worth noting is that the sample itself was not necessarily representative of the general U.S. population (lower income than average, largely Hispanic).

By the end of the study, 39 percent of couples were divorced. When all six of the key predictor variables listed above were used together to estimate who got divorced, the evidence pointed to the wife’s vulnerabilities as the only statistically significant predictor of divorce. The wife’s vulnerabilities also predicted a secondary variable measuring how rapidly couples ended their marriage. In other words, the more of these vulnerabilities a wife reported (adverse childhood experiences, physical/sexual abuse, problematic substance use, frequent negative emotions in the top 25 percent of the sample, or not being raised by married parents), the more likely the couple was to divorce, even after accounting for the other five predictors.

According to recent reports, although speculative, the authors propose a few reasons why this finding occurred. Women tend to handle the lion’s share of domestic and emotional labor in marriages. Women also tend to be more responsive to partners’ needs, have better memory and awareness of relationship events, and notice problems more often. In sum, women with more vulnerabilities may be more likely to reach the decision to exit more often and more quickly.

Recent findings suggest that but are vulnerabilities deterministic of divorce? Not quite. The same study found that communication mattered in an crucial way. Among couples who communicated especially well, including more warmth, humor, and effective problem solving, and less hostility, the added divorce risk tied to wives’ vulnerabilities largely disappeared. The baggage women carry into a marriage appears real, but strong interpersonal communication seems to buffer against it. The findings point to two places worth investing in: reducing childhood adversity in the first place and offering couples support that works with those personal histories. Knowing where the risk lies doesn’t seal a couple’s fate. It tells them where to put in the work.

According to recent reports, 1. Amato, P. R. (2010). Research on divorce: Continuing trends and latest developments. Journal of Marriage and Family, 72(3), 650–666.

2. Smith, M. G., Block, J. M., Bradbury, T. N., & Karney, B. R. (2026). Individual, interpersonal, and socioeconomic predictors of divorce: A 12-year prospective study. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology. Advance online publication. https://dx.doi.org/10.1037/pspi0000537.

#5371. College student develops LEGO-like, 3D-printed moon bricks

College student develops LEGO-like, 3D-printed moon bricks

📅 10 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (553 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Popsci

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that A permanent lunar base will require structures resilient enough to withstand everything from cosmic radiation and micro-meteorites to moonquakes.
  • It has been revealed that A college student at the University of Arkansas (U of A) recently had a different idea.
  • Lunar regolith is a tricky material.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that A permanent lunar base will require structures resilient enough to withstand everything from cosmic radiation and micro-meteorites to moonquakes. There are plenty of building materials to choose from on Earth, but they all come with a catch: transportation storage aboard spacecraft is limited, and each additional pound of cargo will promptly ramp up costs. Engineers have spent years experimenting with ways for future astronauts to source local lunar ingredients, including fine moon dust known as regolith. Unfortunately, most require various binding ingredients that must still be sent from back home.

It has been revealed that A college student at the University of Arkansas (U of A) recently had a different idea. In a collaboration with U of A mechanical engineer Wan Shou, Cole McCallum harnessed a specialized method of 3D printing to manufacture LEGO-esque bricks from lunar dust, no binding required. (These aren’t to be confused with LEGO’s actual lunar bricks mockups). Their results published in the journal NPJ Advanced Manufacturing indicate the bricks could be a promising material to investigate as humanity readies itself for a return to the moon.

Lunar regolith is a tricky material. Unlike Earth’s dirt, it doesn’t contain any amount of organic matter. It’s just loose, sharp-edged particles generated by billions’ of years of asteroid and meteor impacts. This means that moon dust can’t bind on its own and requires at least some secondary ingredients.

While an undergraduate at the U of A, McCallum wondered if a specific type of 3D printing called laser powder bed fusion could offer a workaround. In this technique, fine powder is placed on a flat bed, then exposed to a highly powerful laser beam that fuses each microscopic particle together in a process called sintering. The tray bed lowers down to allow another layer of sintered powder, then repeats the steps until a single, solid block is created. Regolith fits the mold perfectly, so to speak.

In a recent development, “There’s nothing else it’s binding to. The regolith powder is binding to itself,” McCallum said in a university profile.

Sources indicate that mcCallum and Shou didn’t have access to actual lunar material, so they obtained Lunar Highlands Regolith Simulant (LHS-1), a commercial material that replicates the moon dust collected by Apollo astronauts during the 1960s and 70s. They ultimately settled on two shapes, one that resembles a cross and another that looks like the letter “H.” The researchers then 3D-printed tiny prototypes measuring a few centimeters wide that they could connect like LEGOs to construct larger structures.

It has been revealed that there are still some crucial caveats to this sintered regolith strategy. McCallum’s blocks are much more porous and weaker than materials containing binders. Additional research is needed to see how the approach works in a vacuum or microgravity, two inescapable hurdles to living on the moon.

According to recent reports, “These structures we’re making can be self-supported. But I would be hesitant to say our process could be used for something that’s supporting other loads at this moment yet,” noted McCallum.

That mentioned, his demonstration that even a basic framework for lunar base bricks is achievable solely with regolith may offer a promising direction for mission engineers.

A Brooklyn Townhouse Celebrates a Forgotten Design Pioneer

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1274 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Architecturaldigest

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that in the early 1920s, the Pittsburgh-based manufacturer Armstrong Cork Company (now Armstrong World Industries) made the prescient move of tapping a young arts educator named Hazel Dell Brown to act as its in-house decorator.
  • Recent findings suggest that for two contemporary artists setting out to renovate a Brooklyn town house for their young family, Brown’s little-known work recently served not only as inspiration but also as a litmus test.
  • A circa 1980 Gio Ponti chandelier crowns the living room, which is furnished with a vintage Vladimir Kagan sectional sofa and a Jens Risom chair upholstered in a custom fabric based on a Macgregor Harp painting; artwork by Rose Marcus and wallpaper by Antoinette Poisson.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that in the early 1920s, the Pittsburgh-based manufacturer Armstrong Cork Company (now Armstrong World Industries) made the prescient move of tapping a young arts educator named Hazel Dell Brown to act as its in-house decorator. Hers would be an under-recognized yet wildly influential career. Over the course of more than three decades, she designed countless rooms for advertisements, booklets, catalogs, and more that showcased the brand’s products, chief among them linoleum flooring. With their bold colors, fearless mix of patterns, and daring pastiche, her interiors shaped an entire generation of homes in the Rust Belt and beyond.

Recent findings suggest that for two contemporary artists setting out to renovate a Brooklyn town house for their young family, Brown’s little-known work recently served not only as inspiration but also as a litmus test. When interviewing architects to take on the project, the couple first presented examples of vintage Armstrong schemes. “A lot of people would take one look and then show me something different,” reflects the wife, who learned about Brown while working on a project in Pittsburgh. Not so in the case of Tal Schori and Rustam Mehta of GRT Architects. The AD100 duo instantly responded to Brown’s surface-heavy approach and inward-facing embrace of small spaces, or as Schori puts it, “rooms within rooms.” As for their interior designer, Penelope August, a friend of the wife’s since preschool—she implicitly passed with flying colors.

A circa 1980 Gio Ponti chandelier crowns the living room, which is furnished with a vintage Vladimir Kagan sectional sofa and a Jens Risom chair upholstered in a custom fabric based on a Macgregor Harp painting; artwork by Rose Marcus and wallpaper by Antoinette Poisson.

The kitchen features art-glass cabinet fronts by Paul Wissmach Glass Organization and a custom terrazzo floor inspired by ancient roman mosaics of unswept debris.

The attic’s custom oak millwork.

Hembus wallpaper in a custom blue distinguishes the primary bedroom; painting (above bed) by Michael Wang.

Sources indicate that the project evolved into a dynamic collaboration as the couple and their team gutted the town house, set in Carroll Gardens and previously renovated in the 1990s. Together they took care to preserve historic details like the original doors and staircase, with its original mahogany newel posts and handrails. Wherever appropriate, they embraced imperfections, filling in the gaps between old floorboards with contrasting tinted epoxy and leaving levels ever so askew. “This house demonstrates signs of age and that’s not a bad thing,” states Schori. Adds Mehta, “As artists, they understood what is and isn’t precious so that the home does not feel overly restored.”.

The backyard was updated by Brook Landscape, with a shed and swing set by GRT Architects.

In the son’s room, shaker-style cabinetry reveals a reading nook.

A refurbished tub from The Demolition Depot anchors the primary bath, which is lined in tiles by Balineum (on walls) and Artistic Tile (on floor).

Recent findings suggest that brown was nothing if not a gleeful problem solver, presenting flexible solutions to the needs of everyday life, often through inventive secondary spaces. (“Your rumpus room can be anything you like” proclaimed one Armstong campaign.) True to that strategy, GRT devised a floor strategy full of versatile surprises. Adjoining the dining room is a cave-like lounge for watching television or just relaxing, with a pass-through to the kitchen for the easy arrival of snacks. Opposite the cookspace—more on that showstopper later—is a cozy breakfast area, with a load-bearing skylight that offers glimpses of the roof terrace (and sometimes curious children) above. And on the second level, a secret passage leads from the primary suite into the library, one column of shelving concealing a door. “All these appendages to the main spaces allow multiple things to happen at once,” claims Schori.

In the daughter’s room, Shaker-style trim is painted in Farrow & Ball’s Blue Ground.

The kids’ bath mixes terrazzo walls with custom floor tiles by Haand.

Oak millwork incorporates vintage Piero Fornasetti panels in the dining room, where Guillerme et Chambron chairs surround an antique farm table; painting by Jo Nigoghossian, and custom fireplace fabricated by Daniel Armitano.

Surfaces and furnishings tend toward the eclectic and one-of-a-kind, with a mix of wallpapers and fabrics, some deadstock, setting the stage for vintage treasures. In the living room, a Vladimir Kagan sectional sofa found at auction doubles as a jungle gym of sorts. The primary bath is anchored by a salvaged earthenware tub, since glazed a light blue to complement the retro checkerboard tiles and scalloped vanity. And the dining room’s custom millwork incorporates a series of midcentury Fornasetti panels. Doorknobs, lighting, motifs, art by their circle of creative friends—it’s all a mishmash. “We liked things independently of how they worked together,” says the wife. Adds August: “It was so fun to stitch all these elements into an old house—I love a space where you come upon something unexpected.”.

A detail of the kitchen’s terrazzo floor demonstrates stone and metal shapes (some abstract, some legible) inspired by detritus.

A custom sofa frames the lounge off the dining room, which has a pass-through to the kitchen; carpet by Stark.

In the living room, a Gretta Johnson painting hangs above the fireplace, which is flanked by artworks by Cletus Johnson (left) and Ted Mineo (near right) and Miles Huston (Far right).

The husband’s office/music room is cocooned in cork; painting (at left, bottom) by MacGregor Harp.

The stairwell’s painted checkerboard floor hints at classic Americana.

In a recent development, floor to floor, the mood shifts. The son’s and daughter’s rooms each riff on classic Shaker woodwork, with rails and built-in cabinetry that respond to the exposed ceiling joists. Enlivened by a splatter-painted floor and celestial configuration of ceiling lights, the plywood-lined attic operates as a kids’ club, craft room, and family theater in one. (How’s that for a rumpus room, Hazel?) Thanks to some clever excavation and engineering on the part of GRT, the combined garden level and cellar is now a double-height studio for the wife, complete with a gantry crane for hoisting heavy sculptures. Outside, meanwhile, Brook Landscape transformed the backyard into a romantic swath of greenery.

Vintage globe lights from a one-time optometry office add a surreal touch to the powder room.

Loose arrangements of greenery frame the steps to the backyard.

GRT Architects combined the garden level and cellar into a double-height art studio with a register of exposed brick.

A vintage Vilhelm Lauritzen ceiling light punctuates the primary bedroom; painting by Margaux Ogden.

As for that kitchen, here the team took inspiration not only from Brown but from two additional touchstones. Cabinet fronts nod to art glass at the Upper East Side’s late great Glaser’s Bake Shop, the salvaged interiors of which August and the wife chanced upon at The Demolition Depot. The floor, meanwhile, riffs on ancient Roman mosaics of unswept detritus, an example of which can be found at the Vatican Museums. “We wanted a kitchen that wouldn’t look bad if it got messy,” indicates the wife. Working closely with GRT and August, she and her husband evolved that historic precedent into a contemporary series of shapes, some abstract and some legible (a knife, a carrot, a wine glass). Rendered in scraps of stone or metal, their forms now appear to float in poured terrazzo.

Sources indicate that “The way artists think about objects and architecture is as a constant work in progress,” says Mehta. “These are visual people with an incredible mental library of references.” Would Brown approve? Without a doubt. As the designer once wrote: “Whatever you do, use your own ideas. Don’t be afraid of them.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Garmin and Waze are teaming up on an interesting new safety feature that could give cyclists a little extra protection when sharing the road with cars – by making cyclists themselves show up in Waze.

Sources indicate that the fresh feature allows cyclists using a compatible Garmin Edge bike computer or Garmin smartwatch to share their location through Garmin’s LiveTrack feature. That location can then appear in real time to nearby drivers using Waze, with cyclists displayed as moving icons on the road.

As someone who recently joined the Garmin family myself with a smartwatch for tracking my cycling, running, and other activities, this is exactly the type of feature I love seeing added to the platform.

I’ve long maintained that safety – or more accurately, the perception that cycling isn’t safe – is one of the biggest impediments to getting more people onto bikes.

Sources indicate that that’s especially true in the US, where cyclists are often forced to share roads with cars instead of enjoying the kind of widespread separated cycling infrastructure found in many more bike-friendly countries. And when a cyclist and a multi-ton vehicle have to occupy the same space, making sure the driver knows that cyclist is there can make a big difference.

Of course, an icon on Waze isn’t going to magically make cycling safe. It won’t replace protected bike lanes, better road design, slower vehicle speeds, or attentive drivers.

It has been revealed that but I can certainly imagine situations where it could help. Riding at night or in poor visibility, approaching a blind curve, or simply traveling on a narrow road where a driver might otherwise come upon a cyclist unexpectedly are all situations where an advance warning could be useful.

The feature is opt-in through Garmin Connect and activates when the cyclist starts an outdoor cycling activity. Garmin says location sharing is temporary and session-based, and that cyclists’ personal information isn’t displayed in Waze. Of course, anyone who uses a personal GPS device has already accepted that their location is shared with Significant Tech in exchange for features they value, but at least we know that any personalized info stays within Garmin instead of proliferating even further.

This is cool but requires both a Garmin product and the Waze app. IMHO better to equip new cars and trucks with bicycle and pedestrian detection.

Garmin LiveTrack itself is free for customers with compatible Garmin devices and previously allowed cyclists to share their live location, speed, route, and other information with friends and family. I’ve used it myself as a safety feature when venturing off-road and on longer solo journeys. The Waze integration essentially expands that safety net to nearby motorists.

There’s obviously one massive limitation: You need to be riding with a compatible Garmin device, and the driver needs to be using Waze.

But with Waze claiming around 200 million owners globally and Garmin being one of the biggest names in cycling computers and fitness watches, that’s not exactly a tiny Venn diagram.

Anything that gives drivers another chance to see cyclists before actually seeing them sounds like a win to me.

‘One-in-a-million’ yellow fish found in Upcoming York

📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (463 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Popsci

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, we’ll call him mellow yellow.
  • Industry observers note that burbots are long fish that weigh about three to five pounds on average, and live in cold rivers and lakes of North America, Europe, and Asia.
  • The team caught the brightly colored fish during a routine aquatic invasive species survey.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, we’ll call him mellow yellow. An “exceptionally rare” yellow-colored burbot (Lota lota) was recently caught by a team of U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service (USFWS) biologists in Oswego Harbor on Lake Ontario in Upstate Latest York.

Industry observers note that burbots are long fish that weigh about three to five pounds on average, and live in cold rivers and lakes of North America, Europe, and Asia. To the naked eye, they appear scaleless, but are actually covered with tiny, almost microscopic scales. What they eat depends on their size. Smaller burbots will eat zooplankton, while bigger burbots prefer to snack on other fish.

The team caught the brightly colored fish during a routine aquatic invasive species survey. It gets its unique color from a rare genetic condition called xanthochromism. A genetic mutation suppresses the normal pigmentation, it produces a yellow-orange appearance instead of the burbot’s usual grey, olive, or tan coloring. In wild fish, xanthochromism is less common than albinism or melanism, making this fish an “especially unusual capture.”.

The burbot is a native species in the Great Lakes, but the USFWS team indicates the discovery highlights the effectiveness of the Service’s Aquatic Invasive Species Early Detection and Monitoring Program. The program uses a multi-gear fish-surveillance strategy to detect certain non-native species in the harbors, rivers, and embayments of the Great Lakes. Early detection of a watchlist species gives fisheries managers the best opportunity to implement prevention and removal measures if invasive species are detected. Since invasive species are often rare when they first enter new waters, the program uses electrofishing, fyke-netting, gill-netting, and environmental DNA (eDNA) analysis to increase the chances that scientists detect an invasive species.

It has been revealed that “The finding is notable because burbot populations in the lake are extremely low, and the species typically inhabit deeper, cooler waters than those found within the harbor,” the USFWS wrote in a statement. “It represents the first documented detection of a burbot during a fisheries survey in Oswego Harbor, although a few angler catches have been reported.”.

The United States Geological Survey (USGS) fisheries biologists, who examined the fish and are familiar with the species, also observed that it was very thin and appeared to be in poor health. It was later sent to the Cornell University College of Veterinary Medicine for a health analysis due to the “unexplained factors contributing to the continued suppression of its population”.

“The discovery could turn out to be lucky for the burbot too; this exceptionally rare fish may provide valuable insight into the health of the species’ populations throughout the basin that can inform management actions,” the USFWS concluded.

Why Cancer Biomarker Testing Is Personal for Mark-Paul Gosselaar

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Now, he’s using that star power to raise awareness about cancer biomarker testing while sharing how he prioritizes his own health and well-being.
  • In a recent development, “Health is a huge thing for my wife and I, and our family,” Gosselaar told Healthline.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Known for his iconic roles on “Saved by the Bell,” “NYPD Blue,” “Franklin & Bash,” and “Found,” Mark-Paul Gosselaar knows how to grab an audience.

Now, he’s using that star power to raise awareness about cancer biomarker testing while sharing how he prioritizes his own health and well-being.

In a recent development, “Health is a huge thing for my wife and I, and our family,” Gosselaar told Healthline. “We are constantly aware of newly introduced technologies.”.

Having seen people in his life navigate cancer diagnoses, Gosselaar is now raising awareness about the role of biomarker testing in cancer treatment through his partnership with AstraZeneca and its Meet Your Mark campaign.

In a recent development, the campaign aims to educate people facing cancer diagnoses and their loved ones about how biomarker testing may help doctors make more informed, personalized treatment decisions. It also encourages patients to discuss testing with their healthcare teams.

“Biomarkers may tell doctors the specific type of cancer present and if targeted therapies or immunotherapy might help,” Mark Socinski, MD, oncologist and Executive Medical Director of the AdventHealth Cancer Institute, told Healthline.

Industry observers note that he explained that biomarkers are typically genes or proteins that doctors measure through blood or tissue tests. They are used to help guide treatment in numerous diseases but are especially powerful tools in many types of cancer.

In a recent development, “They help decode why cancers behave differently, even when two people have the same cancer type,” remarked Socinski. “However, while biomarker testing provides useful information, it does not guarantee a specific outcome.”.

Despite those limitations, Socinski sees promise in the shift from one-size-fits-all cancer treatment to care tailored to each patient’s specific cancer characteristics.

Recent findings suggest that “Biomarker testing does play a critical role here, and it is vital for people to be aware of the potential benefits,” Socinski said. “It may help change the course of a person’s treatment journey.”.

Gosselaar hopes that greater awareness of biomarker testing can help people facing a cancer diagnosis feel more informed about their treatment options.

Sources indicate that “A lot of the time, when a loved one or someone who has been diagnosed with cancer [it can] feel like your world is in a tailspin,” he stated. “I wanted to get the word out for anyone who’s going through a cancer diagnosis, or a caretaker, to know that biomarker testing is an option, because even though two cancers are similar, their tumors can act very differently and biomarker testing may help the medical expert with more personalized treatment.”.

As part of the campaign, Gosselaar took part in a commercial, something he hadn’t done since before his days on “Saved by the Bell.”.

“This was the first time that I actually had to be on set and not be a character; I had to be me talking about this very serious issue,” he said.

While it was a challenging experience, he remarked it was also fulfilling.

Industry observers note that “I enjoyed the process, and to be able to use my platform to be able to spread the word; it means a lot to me,” he said. “I’m very selective of the things that I want to attach myself to, and this seemed like the right fit.”.

He particularly enjoyed recreating Zack Morris’s signature “timeout” gesture from “Saved by the Bell,” which allowed his character to freeze time and speak directly to the camera.

“Using something from the past that was such a symbolic gesture to so many people of my generation that are now my age and possibly going through [cancer] or knowing someone who’s going through [cancer to] direct them to [this campaign], means a lot,” he stated.

Beyond his efforts to raise awareness about cancer biomarker testing, Gosselaar is equally focused on taking care of his own health.

Sources indicate that getting quality sleep is one of his top priorities. He sleeps on a high-tech mattress that monitors sleep stages, heart rate, heart rate variability, and respiratory rate. He also uses a biometric health and fitness tracker, prioritizes healthy eating, and uses saunas and red light therapy.

Recent findings suggest that “We do everything that we possibly can, but I’m less about longevity and more about just living a healthy lifestyle,” Gosselaar mentioned. “I want to continue doing the things that I’ve done since I was a child…without feeling held back by my health.”.

It has been revealed that as he embraces his 50s, he remarked he’d like to live a long life for his children and future grandchildren. He started taking his health seriously in his 40s after undergoing shoulder surgery.

“[It] really made me realize [that] all the damage I had done in my 20s and 30s sort of adds up later in life, and that’s probably something that I would tell the younger me… to preserve a little bit more and take [an] approach that recovery is just as important as the workout because I did not use my recovery very well; it was not a priority for me,” said Gosselaar.

Industry observers note that he also makes time for himself every day. He said doing so makes him a better person and more able to care for his wife and four children.

It has been revealed that “[It’s] something that I believe in; that I need to do something for myself before I can do something for someone else. Or if I do something for someone else, then I have to equalize that by doing something for me,” he said.

Daily physical activity also helps support his mental well-being.

“I need to do something where I challenge myself, and it could be as simple as a walk. It could be as simple as just getting outside and lifting something heavy [or] taking bags of groceries and taking the long way into your house,” Gosselaar stated.

“Like challenging yourself with picking up things, you know, taking backpacks from the car from your kids and seeing if you can carry three in one hand…or going into the gym and spending an hour in the gym, or 30 minutes, or just moving.”.

When he’s in the sauna, he works on breathing and clearing his thoughts.

“Some people need to meditate, some people need to talk to somebody. I encourage all of that because I think all of that helps,” he noted.

“I’ve done them all. I’ve done the cold plunging, I’ve done all that stuff…some of it works, and some of it doesn’t; it’s whatever you believe in. So I just encourage people to stay healthy and move, get outside, and help other people.”.

The Spice Rack Brain Hack

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (843 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Psychologytoday

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Posted November 16, 2026 | Reviewed by Ekua Hagan.
  • “He who controls the spice controls the universe.”—Frank Herbert.
  • Studies are increasingly finding that spices can boost the variety of good microbes in your gut.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Posted November 16, 2026 | Reviewed by Ekua Hagan.

“He who controls the spice controls the universe.”—Frank Herbert.

Spice adds variety to your life. Especially in your microbiome. Studies are increasingly finding that spices can boost the variety of good microbes in your gut. That, in turn, can improve your mood and cognition via the gut-brain axis.

According to recent reports, A study by Regina Lamendella and colleagues, published in The Journal of Nutrition, found that blends of herbs and spices—including cinnamon, ginger, cumin, turmeric, rosemary, oregano, basil, and thyme—increased diversity of the microbiome, a measure of health. The best results were with the participants who got the largest dose of spices—about 1 ½ teaspoons a day.

According to recent reports, what is so great about spices and herbs? Their main attraction is their high levels of polyphenols—plant chemicals that provide flavor and color. People who eat plenty of polyphenol-rich foods can cut their risk of type 2 diabetes in half and improve their heart health.

Recent findings suggest that polyphenols suppress enzymes that activate inflammation. They are also antioxidants, further helping to quell inflammation. Cloves have about 15 percent polyphenols by weight, whereas veggies may have only 0.1 percent. Along with their intrinsic anti-inflammatory effects, polyphenols act as prebiotic fiber, feeding your beneficial gut microbes.

Industry observers note that the researchers saw an increase in microbes that produce butyrate, an amazing substance that nourishes and heals the cells lining your gut, ensuring that they keep toxins and pathogens out of your bloodstream. Butyrate does more: It can travel to the brain, encouraging the growth of newly introduced nerve cells, improving cognition and memory.

The gut-brain axis responds to inflammation by putting you into sickness mode, where you just want to be left alone to lie in bed while your joy evaporates. This behavior is pretty much identical to depression. Depression and anxiety overlap strongly with gut concerns, and psychiatrists are increasingly turning to prebiotics and probiotics to augment other treatments. Microbes that can improve your mood are called psychobiotics. While polyphenols boost good bacteria, they also fight harmful bacteria like C. difficile, Salmonella, and E. coli.

It has been revealed that it's not exactly news that spices are healthy. Some 2,500 years ago, Hippocrates believed that spices like cinnamon, coriander, and saffron had healing powers. Nutmeg was prescribed for flatulence, and enticingly, ginger was used as an aphrodisiac. The Kama Sutra recommends cardamom, ginger, nutmeg, and cloves for a good time. Spices were, and still are, sexy.

Industry observers note that spices were also expensive. In 410 AD, the Visigoths sacked Rome and held it hostage for a ransom of 5,000 pounds of gold and 3,000 pounds of pepper. At the time, spices were as good as gold. In those days, traders conspired to restrict the supply of spices, ensuring high prices. Their trade routes were kept secret, and excess crops were burned. It was a cutthroat business, but smuggled seeds soon cropped up in tropical farms around the world. Today, supply chains are efficient, and spices are far cheaper, so there’s little to stop you from trying some.

Don't be afraid to play with combinations of spices to create your own custom spice blend. Use it as a rub on fish or meat before cooking or sprinkle some spice on food after it’s cooked. Pro tip: Buy spices whole and grind them just before using to get the maximum joy. Spices have a lot of volatile oils that evaporate over time and deplete the magnificent aromas.

Industry observers note that if you have GERD or IBS, start slowly. Spices activate microbes, which can create gas if you overdo it. But over time, your microbes will adjust.

In a recent development, for everyone else, spices are awesome. They may not help you control the universe, but they taste great, and they can improve your mood. Once you get started, you’ll realize that life is too short to be stuck with bland food. Kick it up a notch.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • A pair of California-based engineers have built what they say may be the largest Game Boy Color ever.
  • Recent findings suggest that the console has already appeared at several maker events, where eager kids have punched and kicked its chunky buttons.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that we may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn more ›.

A pair of California-based engineers have built what they say may be the largest Game Boy Color ever. Standing more than nine feet and weighing around 300 pounds, the Pokémon-yellow goliath requires a U-Haul to transport and took over 1,500 collective hours in a makerspace to create. And it isn’t just for show. The giant handheld plays real Game Boy games, thanks to a pixel-perfect display scaled up from the original and software written from scratch. The designers even fabricated an assortment of to-scale accessories, including game cartridges, a cable link, and AA batteries.

Recent findings suggest that the console has already appeared at several maker events, where eager kids have punched and kicked its chunky buttons. It has also prompted plenty of older millennials, in person and online, to reminisce about simpler days. Build videos posted across social media have racked up hundreds of thousands of views. But for co-creator Paige Powell, a veteran prop designer and mechanical engineer, the giant Game Boy also represents something more special: a labor of love and a chance to inspire young girls to start building things themselves.​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​.

Sources indicate that “It [has] felt very weird to me in a very male-dominated world to build something behind the scenes and then give it to [a] guy who then takes credit,” Powell tells Popular Science. “I want people to see women making stuff!”.

Sources indicate that the giant GameBoy is the joint effort of Powell (@whats_paige_making on Instagram) and engineer Nick Alvarez (@nickbuildstuff on Instagram). Powell has a long track record of building props and sets for the YouTube channel Mega Builds and the immersive art tech giant Meow Wolf. Alvarez, meanwhile, specializes in PCB (printed circuit board) design and spent seven years as a full-time engineering manager at an aerospace defense company.

In a recent development, the two crossed paths while working at the Davis makerspace, just west of Sacramento. Alvarez was building a large LED wall (the kind used for screens at sports arenas) and wanted to hook up Nintendo controllers so it could play games. Piggybacking off of that, Powell proposed taking the idea a step further: a giant playable Game Boy. From there, it only made sense to try and make the world’s largest. That sent them down a rabbit hole that would consume a sizable chunk of their lives (and finances) over the months to follow.

A quick bit of research revealed they weren’t the first one with this idea. Guinness World Records actually has an official entry for the Largest Game Boy Color, an accolade claimed in 2022 by a YouTuber named Jake Carlini. His version measured in at seven feet tall. But calling that one a real Game Boy is quite a stretch. It was really little more than a few pieces of vaguely detailed plywood. Alvarez and Powell realized there was an opportunity, not just to break the record, but to build something far more ambitious.

Industry observers note that “It [the Carlini model] was just kind of [a] slapstick way of putting it together, and we were like, ‘dude, what is this?’ Alvarez claims. ”We can do something actually amazing with our background and our skillset.”.

From the outset, the duo gave themselves a set of constraints to build around. Their Game Boy had to be to scale to the original and functional as a game console. They also committed to making the screen pixel perfect to the 1998 original.

“Everything was built around the constraint of what the screen was going to be,” Powell says.

Recent findings suggest that fortunately, they had some help along the way. When they told Tim Keller, the head of the Davis makerspace, about the project, he agreed to let them set up shop and use the space’s CNC mills, 3D printers, laser cutters, and other equipment.

Industry observers note that with goals set and tools secured, the pair then created a 3D model of their scaled-up Game Boy, starting with a smaller (though still shockingly large) 5.7-foot version. Powell quickly realized that the toughest part to fabricate wasn’t actually the console’s iconic front, but rather its geometrically odd-shaped back shell. The top of the backside starts out flat but then bulges out into a sloped shape toward the bottom where a person would hold it in their palm. The cartridge slot where the game slides into also juts out from the back, adding even more complexity.

Recent findings suggest that once the 3D model was complete, Powell began building the physical body, made mostly of plywood shaped on the CNC machine, an automated manufacturing device that reads computer code and uses that to control cutting machines like mills, lathes, and lasers. CNC machines are indispensable tools in many makers’ arsenals. But a project like this requires adaptability. Partway through, Powell claims, she realized the CNC machine wasn’t all that well suited to making square cuts, which meant the final product would need more hand carpentry than initially planned.

In a recent development, meanwhile, Alvarez was hard at work perfecting the display and electronics under the hood (or, in this case, the shell). He built the screen from a series of HUB75 LED panels, the kind commonly used in large digital signs. The trick was getting his massive DIY display to scale up accurately from the original GameBoy’s 160-by-144 pixel screen. He also used a small microcontroller (essentially a tiny computer assigned to a specific task) to map all of the device’s buttons and switches.

When the giant Game Boy plays games, it’s running them on a specialized emulator rather than the physical game cartridge that gets slotted into the device. The emulator is a piece of software that imitates a Game Boy. Emulators are common these days and are what let hobbyists play old Nintendo games on smartphones.

Sources indicate that the to-scale cartridges Powell and Alvarez fabricated are really more for show. That means, theoretically, their device can run any Game Boy game. Alvarez says he even built in a feature that cycles to a different game each time the power is switched on. So far, the pair have posted videos of the device playing Pokémon and Donkey Kong. Alvarez even watched The Odyssey on it.

Powell and Alvarez have shown off their creations at two events so far: Open Sauce in 2026 and the Bay Area Maker Fair in Vallejo, California. Getting the Game Boys there was a task in itself. The larger of the two (around 300 pounds) required a large U-Haul and four people just to load it. Once unloaded, they faced a more daunting challenge: the wrath of children. Drawn in by the device’s giant buttons, kids at the events let loose.

“Kids were coming up and karate-kicking them, and I was just like, ‘Oh my God, man,’” Powell states.

Alvarez concurs. “They were punching the crap out of the buttons.”.

In a testament to its build quality, the giant Game Boy withstood the onslaught of toddler haymakers. Those who weren’t assailing the device were often absorbing an emotional gut punch of their own. Both in person and online, fans told Powell and Alvarez how the build brought back childhood memories. One commenter recalled how seeing it reminded them of a time at a school when a bully stole their beloved Game Boy. Decades later, he said, he’s still mad.

It has been revealed that looking ahead, Powell and Alvarez hope to find their creation a upcoming home where it can be on display and accessible to the public. They’d like to recoup some of the money they’ve poured into it, but Powell also expressed some wariness of it winding up locked away in some buyer’s private collection. Ideally, she says, it would land in a museum of some kind, where it could inspire the next generation of budding makers.
